content_en:
## **In Brief:**

- Following CEO Tim Sweeney’s announcement of a “huge pivot” towards AI tools, Epic Games has confirmed that AI tools are now being used to develop code and features for Unreal Engine 6 and Unreal Editor for Fortnite \[UEFN\]
- Epic’s Executive Vice President of Development, Marcus Wassmer, told *This Week in Videogames* in a statement that AI tools are “helping across a broad spectrum of development”
- When asked if Epic was concerned about the reaction from those skeptical about AI being used to develop Unreal Engine, Wassmer said: “We are more concerned about the risks of moving too slowly than we are about AI skepticism”

Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney has stated on social media that the company is using AI tools to “develop code for Unreal Engine.” Epic has confirmed this in a statement provided to *This Week in Videogames*.

This follows Sweeney’s announcement earlier in October 2026 that the company is experiencing a “huge pivot” to “retool for maximum AI acceleration.”

In a Twitter reply to ‘BenjiGameDev’ back in November 2025, Sweeney denied assumptions that Epic was using AI tools to improve, update, and build features for Unreal Engine (UE).

Revisiting their assumptions in a 23 October 2026 tweet – which comes after Sweeney’s AI pivot announcement and the release of a vibe coded update to the Epic Games Launcher – BenjiGameDev asks if “AI tools \[are\] being used to develop UE now?”

Sweeney replies: “Yes, we are now using AI tools to develop code for Unreal Engine.”

Given the Epic Games Launcher update, the reports that an upcoming shooter using Disney IP was given a “no hand-written code” mandate, and Epic previously announcing that the upcoming Unreal Engine 6 would be built with AI tool integration in mind, it may be unsurprising that Epic is also using AI to develop its widely adopted game engine itself.

In Epic’s June 2026 Road to UE6 blog post, it also stated that internal teams, including the engine’s engineering team, had been investigating “what works and what doesn’t for code generation.”

“What’s interesting is that most of these use cases aren’t even generating mainline Unreal Engine code, though that will probably come eventually as well,” the blog post said at the time.

After reaching out to Epic with several related questions, *This Week in Videogames* received responses from Executive Vice President of Development Marcus Wassmer.

“As we mentioned back at Unreal Fest in Chicago on stage and in interviews, we are definitely using AI to develop code and features for Unreal Engine,” Wassmer said. “Almost all development happening right now is being done in the dev streams attached to *Fortnite*, UEFN \[Unreal Editor for Fortnite\], and UE6. There’s a possibility of a 5.9. If we make it, it would be a relatively modest update for specific systems and will include changes developed with AI. Generally speaking though we’re working as hard as we can on UEFN and UE6.”

When asked about the specific AI tools being used and how they were being deployed to develop and improve Unreal Engine, Wassmer said:

“There are a number of tools in use but probably the most obvious ones are Claude Code and Codex with their associated AI models. They’re helping across a broad spectrum of development, with some particularly big recent wins being almost the complete elimination of non-deterministic cooking bugs which we’ve been fighting for a decade and an acceleration of work related to compressing shaders which both significantly reduce patch sizes. \[Other wins include\] a rewrite of a significant portion of the D3D12 rendering layer (which I estimated as needing three to six weeks of work for a single engineer, but the work was actually completed in about one week with a nice win on CPU time and fewer bugs), lots of help in keeping our internal test suites healthy as well as expanding those test suites for more coverage, etc.

“Not only that, we’ve started deploying automatic monitoring of PC stability on *Fortnite* that’s already detecting issues with specific driver/hardware combinations and features that would previously have taken months to root cause, as well as automatic root cause analysis and automatic fix generation that together have started to measurably improve the long tail of gnarly PC issues in *Fortnite* and Unreal Engine.”

“Another area of note is that we’re more able to take on some larger architectural refactors with AI than we were able to before. Developers can expect the engine to end up significantly more modular for faster iteration times, and with more ability to strip out what you don’t need from UE on a particular game. These are refactors we’ve wanted to do for a while, but they’ve involved changing thousands of files in relatively minor ways in each instance, and in bulk, \[it\] was too big a task to effectively tackle by hand.

“The tools are helping us not just develop code and features, but to keep the engine more stable as we work, trim, and streamline it, and really modernise it in a way that we haven’t been able to before given the size, complexity, and age of the engine code.”

Following on from the Epic Games Launcher update, *TWIV* also asked if elements of Unreal Engine development are being vibe coded.

*This Week in Videogames is **funded entirely by readers**, which lets us resist advertising and commercial interests. Become a paid supporter today and get access to original feature articles, comments, a community Discord, newsletters, and more while backing truly independent games coverage.*

“Yes, we are vibe-coding things,” Wassmer responded. “That means our engineers are no longer writing the bulk of the code, but they are still guiding the tools to get the architectural result we want. We’re not ‘one-shotting’ the engine; we’re iterating with AI to ship features developers want and keep the engine within the memory, performance, and scalability envelopes.”

Summarising the benefits the Unreal Engine team has seen by using AI, Wassmer said: “Faster development of individual features and tasks, fewer bugs, more test coverage, performance improvements, patch size reductions, and really the ability for our engineers to explore ideas they’ve had to reduce tech debt and improve features for a long time, but not had the time to tackle. We’re seeing that last area really start to take off as the tools get better and people get more familiar with using them.”

*TWIV* also asked Epic whether it was concerned about the reaction of AI-skeptic consumers or developers that build their games with Unreal.

“We are more concerned about the risks of moving too slowly than we are about AI skepticism,” Wassmer said. “We think that in pretty short order doing AI development for basically all software will be ubiquitous because software done correctly with AI will simply be better and be more capable of responding quickly to customer feedback than software done without. The best way to counter any skepticism is through the quality of the games and tools we’re able to deliver.

“Building on 30 years of foundational code, our engine developers are now able to solve challenging problems much quicker. AI is also helping us identify and fix issues with engine code faster and more reliably, while shipping new features with minimal regressions. Ultimately this translates into the acceleration of new features in Unreal Engine with improved stability and faster iteration times, enabling developers to build more ambitious games on accelerated timelines. And with Unreal Engine’s source code availability, the adoption of AI tools will help developers customise the engine to meet the specific needs of their games more efficiently.

“We don’t think it’s viable to take a halfway approach to AI in development. We think it’s best to just be up front with what we’re doing, share best practices with other developers, and make the best UE6 we can with the best tools available at any given time.”

### Regal debuts Goal Oriented Agents, putting an actor and a director model on every call

Enterprise voice artificial intelligence company Regal Voice Inc. today added Goal Oriented Agents to its platform, enabling businesses using them to define what a call has to accomplish, and providing two AI models that split the work of getting there.

The new agents are aimed at a problem Regal says shows up in calls such as auto insurance claims, in which someone reporting an accident tends to explain what happened, where and who was involved in one go. Agents built on conditional logic often circle back for details the caller already gave, just so each field gets filled. Building the whole agent on a single prompt keeps the conversation open, and in Regal’s view it leaves business processes only loosely followed.

Goal Oriented Agents put two models on each call. Regal calls them an actor and a director, and both start work as soon as the caller stops talking. The actor, a smaller and faster model tuned for dialogue, replies right away. Running behind it, the director checks whether the goals for the current stage have been met and can move the call to a new stage with fresh instructions for the actor.

Businesses build the agents out of goal nodes, each listing the goals to be met by the end of the node and any prerequisites that come first. Booking a callback can count as one of those goals. A prerequisite is something the agent has to establish before it can act, such as the caller’s date of birth. Regal said those can be written as plain-language conditions too, for example “the caller mentioned a death in the family.”

The director reviews progress after every turn, so one answer can tick off several items at once. Regal’s sample auto insurance claim has a caller named Dan describing the vehicle damage, photo evidence and injuries in his first message. All three get marked as collected, and the agent goes straight to his name. Once it has that, the director sees location and policy number are still missing, so the actor’s next question is where he is.

Regal said complex intake and qualification calls are among the strongest uses it has seen for the agents. The company named Medicare enrollment, roadside assistance and mortgage qualification as uses the design opens up. Medical intake that complies with the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act is another.

Google LLC, AAA and Toyota Motor Corp. are among the more than 200 enterprises Regal says it serves. Customers of Five9 Inc.’s contact center platform gained access to Regal’s voice agents through an integration in August.

Regal is a venture capital-backed startup that has raised $83 million to date. That includes a $40 million round in October 2024.

content_en:
**VUSE XR**, a Freiburg-based startup developing enterprise software for mixed reality training, today announced the closing of a €1.2 million pre-Seed financing round.

The round was led by IACD, a Düsseldorf-based business angel network, with additional participation from individual business angels.

“*From an investor’s perspective, VUSE XR brings together everything we look for at this stage: an exceptional team, defensible AI-driven technology, and strong commercial traction. The company has demonstrated its ability to turn a technically demanding product into a scalable software business with considerable growth potential, further accelerated by continuous AI-powered feature enrichment*,” said **Markus Roithmeier**, IACD member and Chairman of the VUSE XR Advisory Board.

Founded in November 2023 by cousins Niclas Matthias and Dr. Paul Matthias, VUSE XR develops the VUSE XR Hub, an enterprise software platform that enables industrial and life sciences companies to create, manage and deploy immersive mixed reality training for complex products and processes.

While mixed reality hardware has matured rapidly, producing the training content to run on it has remained expensive and difficult to scale; VUSE XR is addressing this problem. The startup replaces the traditional model of costly, agency-led custom mixed reality projects with a standardised, AI-assisted workflow that allows companies to build, update and distribute training content themselves, across products and locations.

The biggest selling point here is the ease with which VUSE XR helps enterprises to create mixed reality training content. The VUSE XR Hub works by converting existing CAD models, engineering data and product documentation into photorealistic 3D models, which users can then arrange into interactive training sequences using AI-assisted tools or drag-and-drop functionality.

“*Mixed reality hardware is advancing rapidly, but creating mixed reality training content remains the biggest barrier to broader enterprise adoption. The VUSE XR Hub removes this bottleneck, enabling companies to unlock significant business value from mixed reality*,” said **Niclas Matthias**, co-founder and Chief Executive Officer of VUSE XR.

Once the content is created, training can be delivered via a web browser, mobile devices, or fully immersive XR headsets such as Meta Quest. The results are tracked centrally, and content can be updated and redeployed across an organisation at any time.

The company already counts some of the major names in the industrial and life sciences space as its customers. Its customer base includes ZEISS, Hologic, Badenova, Scheidt & Bachmann, WITRON, University Medical Centre Hamburg-Eppendorf (UKE) and Sartorius. VUSE XR has won the smartXautomation Award 2025, the AI Champions Award 2025 from the German state of Baden-Württemberg, and the pitch competition at Black Forest Space 2026.

**Andreas Goss**, IACD member and former Chief Executive Officer of thyssenkrupp Steel, said, *“Effective training is critical to productivity, knowledge transfer and the safe operation of increasingly complex products and processes. The technology developed by VUSE XR has the potential to fundamentally change how companies deliver training, making it more accessible and scalable across products and locations.”*

Alongside the funding, VUSE XR is strengthening its commercial leadership team with two senior appointments: Jan Hendrik Degner, who joins as Chief Commercial Officer, bringing experience from J.P. Morgan and CEWE Group, and Robert Günther, whose background includes senior positions at Meta and Unity, takes the role of Vice President of Sales and Service Delivery.

The startup says it will use the pre-Seed capital to advance its enterprise mixed reality training platform VUSE XR Hub, expand its AI-assisted creation capabilities and accelerate commercial growth. “*With this funding and our expanded commercial team, we are ready to build VUSE XR into the category leader in enterprise mixed reality training*,” Matthias added.

content_en:
### Edge Sound raises $2M to help physical AI make sense of audio

Edge Sound Research Inc. today announced it has raised $2 million in new funding to build audio infrastructure that isolates useful sounds and combines them with other sensor data to help physical AI systems understand what’s happening in real time.

Stormbreaker Ventures led the round, bringing the company’s total funding to $9 million.

When the company first approached this problem, it looked at sports. When a basketball hits the court, fans are stomping in the stands and bass pounds through the arena’s speakers – all of this comes through microphones at the same time. For an artificial intelligence system trying to isolate the dribble, those overlapping sounds can make this difficult.

This challenge sits at the center of Edge Sound Research’s approach to machine perception: connecting audio with tracking and visual data to determine which sound belongs to which object.

“The issue in audio is it’s not object oriented; it’s channel oriented,” co-founder and Chief Executive Valtteri Salomaki told SiliconANGLE in an interview.

For broadcasters, making that connection means following a player’s sounds through a crowded arena. Edge is betting the same approach could help robots and other physical AI systems interpret the world around them — including activity their cameras cannot yet see.

Humans do this automatically because we exist in a multimodal world: Sight, sound and physical sensation all come in at once. In the physical AI world, sound has always been treated as a second-class citizen to vision because cameras are already everywhere, in everyday life and used for everything. For humans, sound is fundamental to navigating everywhere.

Audio comes in channels, Salomaki explained. It’s connected to microphones, which are positioned around a space or on objects and they listen in locations. These produce signals that identify sounds – they don’t directly associate with anything until something else turns them into readily identifiable information.

“It’s split into two layers,” Salomaki said. “One is how do you create a digital twin of all sensors. The other one is how do you create AI machine learning models to source separate sound elements.”

In the sports arena demonstration, the system uses microphone locations, pickup patterns and player tracking to select useful audio. It then associates locations; visual and audio are paired to identify objects — such as players, the ball, even the coach or a referee with the whistle.

The company said users can import 3D spaces or 2D layouts with coordinates and place sensors within that representation. This allows a spatial map of the environment and its sensors; this is essentially the “digital twin” that Salomaki is referring to.

Other use cases could involve autonomous vehicles, which could be given digital ears to hear if a siren is approaching. Humans identify sounds and direction because our ears are on the sides of our heads. If a sound comes from the left, it’s louder on that side, even if we can’t see an object there.

Anyone who has heard a siren approaching or receding has also experienced the Doppler effect, where the pitch increases or decreases depending on how fast it’s coming or going. A higher pitch can give an autonomous vehicle an immediate warning that an emergency vehicle is approaching from a blind corner (and its direction of approach), even if the lights aren’t visible on camera.

**Building the models for audio perception**

Edge has a general model that it develops and fine-tunes for customer needs. These models face different delay target requirements for real-time activity. Salomaki cited a sub-33-millisecond tolerance for sports broadcasting and said other environments might tolerate 100 or 200 milliseconds.

Useful perception needs to arrive on time for most applications because hearing what happens needs to be paired with seeing.

The company is building toward hardware independence with its digital twin software and AI models, allowing Edge to assemble new applications around a core technology. This way, it will become audio infrastructure that will work alongside existing microphones and cameras customers already have for their current physical AI robots, media and other systems.

With the funding, Salomaki said, Edge will complete integration with existing enterprise customers and make the platform’s components transferable across industries ahead of a Series A.

Live sports has already given Edge a commercial market as it developed and validated its perception technology, using that to help train and build its models. Its Virtual Sound Engine, which automatically captures and isolates sound from complex environments, is already deployed commercially across the industry. Customers and partners include American audio equipment manufacturer Shure Inc., the National Basketball Association, Fox Sports Media Group and the United States Tennis Association Inc.

“In order to achieve the result everybody wants in physical AI, computers need to become a little bit more human,” Salomaki said.

### Crux Labs raises over $6M to improve enterprise agents with human judgment

Crux Labs, an artificial intelligence platform turning enterprise judgment into continuous agent improvement, launched today with over $6 million in funding.

Benchstrength and Misneach led the round, with participation from Analog Ventures and Pareto Holdings.

The scale of enterprise AI agents in deployment can range from thousands to millions of user interactions per day. Existing observability platforms make agentic traces easier for humans to monitor and inspect, but make it difficult to improve agent behavior at higher volumes.

Many teams end up sampling the top 1% or less of traces for manual review based on a particular metric, threshold or random selection, meaning that the vast majority of agent failures pass by.

“Aligning AI agents to human judgment is one of the biggest challenges of our time,” said co-founder and Chief Executive Julie Kheyfets (pictured, left). “Agents are incredible at attaining goals, but they lack access to the years of heuristics that we as humans have collected in our heads.”

From the company’s point of view, if “what good looks like” exists in the heads of experts, chances are that fixes will always arrive late. This could mean weeks passing between a problem appearing as a small glitch and escalating to the point where a ticket is entered into the system and a patch eventually applied. This cycle can be greatly reduced if the experts and the AI agents are on the same level.

Crux uses its own agents to address this challenge by acting as evaluators and an improvement team. They capture employees’ expert judgment and calibrate it across millions of interactions, so workers don’t need to look at a tiny sample to understand what’s happening. They can amplify their own judgment across a larger segment.

The company said it has seen strong traction for its platform across high-growth startups and Fortune 500 businesses in healthcare, cybersecurity, financial services, and other complex industries.

“Engineering teams know how to build AI agents, and subject matter experts know what success looks like, but enterprises lack the bridge between them,” said co-founder and Chief Technology Officer Krishna Kulkarni (right).

### Solink raises more than $100M to pull business data from security cameras with AI

Video intelligence company Solink Corp. revealed today that it has raised more than $100 million in new funding.

Solink started out in Ottawa in 2009 selling cloud video surveillance, and its software now uses artificial intelligence to pull information out of the security cameras retailers, restaurants and warehouse operators already have installed. The company said the new money will fund its roadmap for what it calls AI vision intelligence. By its own count, about 500,000 cameras at more than 35,000 customer locations in 65 countries now feed into the platform.

The company added AI agents for perimeter security and loss prevention work in February. Those agents run on edge devices and do not need proprietary cameras. The VerifEye command center that Solink sells to security operations centers gained vision language models a month later, with the aim of filtering out false alarms before an operator ever sees them.

Nobody should need to watch footage to know what is happening inside a business, in the view of co-founder and Chief Executive Mike Matta. He called the present a “watershed moment” for physical businesses. With the new money, Matta said, Solink wants to help customers reduce loss and uncover revenue from their existing cameras.

Toronto-based private equity firm Vertu Capital led the round. Goldman Sachs Group Inc. also put in a material amount through Growth Equity at Goldman Sachs Alternatives, according to Solink. The bank’s asset management arm led the company’s $60 million Series C round in July 2023. Golub Growth and Comcast Ventures came in as new investors.

Eric Kafka, a partner at Vertu, called AI vision intelligence “one of the most significant opportunities in software today.” Solink, he said, has shown the foresight and execution needed to define the category. Customer adoption and the product roadmap made coming back “a natural decision,” said Mike Reilly, a managing director in Goldman’s growth equity group.

Solink did not disclose a valuation, and it gave no detail on the strategic opportunities it also plans to fund with part of the round. Including the new funding, investors have now put more than $198 million into the company.

title_en: Sources: an Accenture staffer's Claude agent ran on a DOD network for two months and appears to have sent info to a third-party site before it was identified
excerpt_en: Sources: an Accenture staffer's Claude agent ran on a DOD network for two months and appears to have sent info to a third-party site before it was identified
content_en:
Earlier this year, sources tell WIRED, a contractor caused a security incident at the Department of Defense by connecting a secure centralized system used by multiple intelligence agencies to their personal account for Claude Code, Anthropic’s AI coding agent. It appears that the agent used by the contractor, who is employed by global consulting firm Accenture, then sent information about the DOD system, including login credentials, to a high-risk third-party website.

The centralized system contains controlled unclassified information (CUI), which is considered sensitive and not to be released to the public without review. CUI can include information about critical infrastructure, nuclear submarine propulsion, and vulnerabilities to chemical and biological terrorism. Additionally, security experts say, access to the system could allow for the exploitation of even more sensitive ones.

“It puts all the data that’s in there at risk,” says a source aware of the incident, who requested anonymity as they were not authorized to speak to the press. If the third-party software was compromised, “there could be somebody out there with the ability to log into a secure environment without anyone knowing. It’s 100 percent a national security threat and could cause irreparable harm.”

A DOD spokesperson tells WIRED that “the Department does not comment on the status of its networks or systems.”

“We take all concerns seriously. These allegations were thoroughly and independently investigated and found to be without merit. We fully complied with our legal and contractual obligations,” an Accenture spokesperson tells WIRED. When pressed, Accenture didn’t offer clarification on who conducted the investigation, or dispute that had been what could be characterized as an incident.

The Accenture employee is alleged to have connected a secure production environment to their personal Claude account so as to allow an AI agent to write and deploy code. Claude is currently barred from being used by DOD staff. (Anthropic directed WIRED to the company’s usage policy**,** which instructs users not to use its products to “interfere with the operation of military bases and related infrastructure” or to “bypass security controls such as authentication systems, end point protection, or monitoring tools without authorization.”)

The Accenture employee’s AI agent ran on the DOD network for two months before it was identified and the vulnerability could be patched. Sources indicate that despite the security risks posed by the AI coding agent, Accenture employees did not treat the incident as severe or urgent. DOD employees and federal contractors are required to report any cybersecurity incident within 72 hours of its discovery, but sources indicate Accenture did not initially report the breach to the government at all.

“We are in a conflict with Iran right now,” says the employee, noting that Iran has attempted to hack several federal agencies and parts of US infrastructure. “It’s the worst time to be having this kind of cavalier attitude.”

Accenture currently has more than $3.5 billion in contracts with the federal government, nearly $605 million of which are with the DOD. The company also contracts with other federal agencies, such as the Department of Education, the General Services Administration, and the Department of Energy, among others. Earlier this month, the Federal Bureau of Investigation found that an Accenture contractor failed to patch a vulnerability that led to the hacking group ShinyHunters getting access to the details of thousands of the Bureau’s employees. The FBI removed that contractor in early October.

Matt Triner, founder of Hunter Strategy, a Washington, DC-based IT consulting company, says that the issue exemplifies the conflicting demands government contractors face more broadly. “Organizations are often punished for reporting incidents like this, even though it’s the right and legal thing to do,” says Triner. In many cases, he says, a company could lose government contracts by admitting they’ve had a security breach, though he says that an incident like the one described is “absolutely one that would need to be reported.”

Triner also notes that the increasing pressure on contractors to deliver projects faster and at a lower price point is at odds with prioritizing safety and security. “Unfortunately, everyone is operating in a system where there are competing rules and incentives, and that existed before AI, but now it’s the same problem on speed,” says Triner.

The coding environment accessed by the Accenture contractor is run on the Non-classified Internet Protocol Router Network (NIPRNet), a DOD network used for unclassified information. While it does connect to the internet—contractors and employees can access their emails and web browsers through the network—it is heavily secured.

According to the source, in order to automate the process of writing code and spinning up cloud servers, the contractor gave their login credentials to the Claude agent. This gave the agent administrative access and allowed it to bypass the security controls enforced through the normal login process. The AI agent—which was not only writing code but also committing it or saving the code into the system on behalf of the Accenture employee—needed to connect out to the internet to perform its tasks. In doing so, it appears to have sent the contractor’s login credentials, passwords, and a map of NIPRNet out to a third party website.

WIRED is declining to name the third party website so as to protect the system from further vulnerability, but National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) has previously identified it as high risk because it has a vulnerability that could let hackers inject instructions into an AI coding agent to steal credentials.

The system the AI agent accessed contained CUI. “Information from a CUI environment is not supposed to leave that infrastructure,” says the source. “There is no insight about what happened to the information, including the login credentials, after it was sent to \[that service\], whether it’s been retained”

Depending on the agency and its work, CUI can include anything from personally identifiable information (PII) to proprietary business or contracting information. According to the DOD’s website, CUI can include information on “the securing and safeguarding of explosives, hazardous chemicals, or pipelines,” documentation related to the designs of “military or space equipment or technology;” and “the exact location and quantities of radioactive material.”

Distinct from the actual data, a map of it could be incredibly valuable to a hacker. “Once an attacker understands how those things fit together, even if those things are public information, what is sensitive is how we are putting those things together and turning that into actionable intelligence,” says Triner.

While a map might not get a hacker into a system, he says, it could help an adversary move faster once they do have access and “help an attacker understand where the crown jewels are.”

Jake Williams, a former NSA hacker and faculty at IANS, an intelligence and security consultancy, says that an AI agent running code in NIPRNet presents a “huge problem, and there are huge national security impacts.”

Williams notes that while individual pieces of data or information might be considered CUI, “when that unclassified information is aggregated, that can become classified itself.” For instance, the location of certain hazardous materials might be CUI, as might be information about the vulnerability of the facilities that house them. Combined, however, they could reveal information that would be kept classified.

title: An updated Model Spec for more capable and beneficial AI
excerpt: OpenAI’s updated Model Spec outlines five core values to guide more capable AI toward sound judgment, human agency, and faithfulness to human intent.
title_en: An updated Model Spec for more capable and beneficial AI
excerpt_en: OpenAI’s updated Model Spec outlines five core values to guide more capable AI toward sound judgment, human agency, and faithfulness to human intent.
content_en:
# An updated Model Spec for more capable and beneficial AI

As our models get smarter and take more consequential actions in the world, it becomes increasingly important that they go beyond just interpreting the specific instructions they receive. Models also need to understand human intentions and values, so they can exercise good judgment in situations their instructions don’t explicitly address while remaining faithful to human intent and oversight.

Today we’re updating the <u>Model Spec</u>(opens in a new window), our public description of how we want our models to behave. The update reorganizes its guidance around five underlying values: **faithfulness to human intent**, **harm minimization**, **honesty and transparency**, **human agency**, and **care**. This reflects an aim of our work on <u>value alignment</u>: for models to understand and apply human values in unfamiliar situations, while remaining faithful to human intent. Alongside clearer explanations of existing principles, the revision adds guidance on context, oversight, and agency, adjusts some behavioral defaults, and retires much of the detailed style guidance.

The five values above articulate broad commitments already reflected across the Model Spec: serving human purposes, being truthful, minimizing harm, respecting people’s freedom to form their own views, and taking their circumstances seriously. Bringing these commitments together helps explain why the Spec asks models to behave as it does, and helps us develop clearer guidance where those commitments were less fully expressed. This update is another step in our <u>work to refine the Spec</u> through research, experience deploying models, <u>public feedback</u> on the Spec and model behavior, and discussions with users and outside experts.

We want AI to benefit a world of people with different needs, values, and hopes for the future.

**Faithfulness to human intent** is the foundation of this approach: understanding and helping people pursue what matters to them. OpenAI writes the Spec, sets boundaries, and trains models to respect them; developers direct applications within those boundaries; and users direct the model’s work subject to those constraints. Our models should <u>expand people’s ability to shape their own lives</u> by helping them understand the world, discover possibilities, and pursue the goals they choose, while taking seriously how that assistance affects others. Faithfulness to human intent and the remaining four values organize the Spec and guide how our models should navigate some of the most important trade-offs they face. They are not intended to capture the full range of human values our models should respect and help people pursue.

Faithfulness means going beyond following instructions literally to deeply understanding what OpenAI, developers, and users intend and value, and acting wisely when that understanding is incomplete. It also means recognizing that people’s beliefs and values can change, and helping them reflect and grow in ways they would endorse without quietly steering them or overriding their choices. For example, when helping someone compare job offers, the model might draw on priorities they have shared before—such as predictable hours—while making those assumptions visible and easy to correct.

Our mission is to ensure that artificial general intelligence benefits all of humanity. This requires considering not only someone’s immediate intentions, but also their longer-term interests and the effects on others. The other four values make these considerations explicit:

- **Minimizing harm** means respecting firm safety boundaries and accounting for the foreseeable consequences of the model’s actions.
- **Honesty and transparency** mean being truthful about what the model knows, does, and is uncertain about so people can understand and evaluate its reasoning and work.
- **Facilitating human agency** means strengthening people’s ability to understand, choose, and act for themselves.
- **Care** means attending to the circumstances of those affected, following relevant social and professional norms, and doing work people can rely on.

The Spec turns these values into practical guidance, with firm boundaries where needed to protect people and society, and otherwise mostly takes the form of defaults that users and developers can override.

Alongside this Model Spec update, we’ve been exploring new training methods to help our models learn these core values and better understand and follow the Spec’s specific behavioral principles. The aim is to build an understanding of why those principles matter and how to apply them in new situations: to do the *right things for the right reasons*. We want that understanding to support sound judgment in consequential decisions and care in everyday decisions that can add up to <u>lasting benefits for people and society</u>(opens in a new window). We’ll share results and lessons from this training work in future updates.

This reorganization also helped us identify where additional guidance was needed, develop new principles to address it, and revise or retire existing guidance as needed.

The new section on faithfulness to human intent starts from the idea that what people value is primary, and instructions are ordinarily the clearest and most important signals of those values. This approach borrows from the assistance-games framing of alignment (see <u>early work</u>(opens in a new window) and a <u>later overview</u>(opens in a new window)). The section incorporates an updated <u>chain of command</u>(opens in a new window), which explains which instructions apply and how conflicts are resolved. A new subsection, <u>consider context carefully</u>(opens in a new window), explains how conversations, memories, and other contextual evidence should inform the model’s understanding of people’s intentions and preferences.

We’ve also added defaults on <u>supporting human agency</u>(opens in a new window) and <u>following relevant social norms</u>(opens in a new window), and expanded existing guidance on <u>controlling and communicating side effects</u>(opens in a new window). These principles capture additional, often subtle but important ways the remaining values should surface in model behavior: considering the effects of the work on others, strengthening users’ capabilities, and producing work people can rely on, while respecting the user’s goals and instructions.

At the same time, we’re retiring most of the Spec’s detailed style guidance. Style should adapt to what people prefer—in aggregate, within languages and cultures, and for each person—with user feedback and context providing evidence about those preferences. The Spec retains stronger defaults, such as <u>approaching questions objectively</u>(opens in a new window). Users and developers can explicitly ask the model to take a particular perspective, but the model should not infer that preference merely from what it thinks they want to hear.

Finally, reflecting the increasing breadth of our models’ use cases and deployment settings, we now refer to the model as “GPT” rather than “the assistant” in the Spec.

This update is a first step in making the values and reasoning behind the Spec more explicit as models become more capable. The Model Spec describes the behavior we are working toward; our models do not yet fully reflect it. We will keep improving both the Spec and the models as we learn from research, real-world use, and feedback.

We want to hear which parts of the Spec you find compelling, where you disagree with the balance it strikes, and what it overlooks or leaves unclear. Feedback on the values, trade-offs, and specific language can help us improve it. We invite you to read the <u>updated Model Spec</u>(opens in a new window) and <u>share your perspective</u>(opens in a new window).

title: Mistral releases the weights for Mistral Large 4, or Le Chonk, and says it rivals top open models such as GLM-5.3 on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index

excerpt_en: Mistral releases the weights for Mistral Large 4, or Le Chonk, and says it rivals top open models such as GLM-5.3 on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index
content_en:
### ZDNET’s key takeaways

- As planned, Mistral has released the weights for its ML4 model.
- ML4 sets a new bar for Western open models.
- Open models are increasingly competitive with proprietary models.

French AI lab Mistral shipped its latest model, Mistral Large 4 (ML4), nicknamed “Le Chonk” for its trillion-parameter size, in preview on Oct. 6. As promised, the lab has released the model’s weights, alongside some new benchmark scores that show Western open models gaining ground over their Chinese peers.

**Also: Open weights vs. closed: An AI civil war’s afoot**

## New coding performance ranking

ML4’s score on the agentic coding benchmark Terminal-Bench 4.0 jumped to 41% from its preview version’s 28% to 41%, beating Opencode’s GLM-5.3 by one small but important point. On the overall Index, however, which shows a model’s composite score across three relevant benchmarks, ML4 is a point behind GLM-5.3, scoring a 48 to GLM-5.3’s 49. Codex GPT-6.1 Terra also scores a 48 overall.

As a reminder, benchmark scores themselves should be taken with a grain of salt, especially considering how many models cheat.

Still, that improvement in performance is meaningful for just a few weeks of extra training. As proprietary AI remains expensive to use, economical models that don’t sacrifice performance are eye-catching. ML4 “rivals top open models such as GLM-5.3 on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index while using 47% less tokens per task on average,” Mistral said.

## Cybersecurity prowess

When Mistral released ML4 in preview earlier this month, it touted how the model prioritizes cyber defense capabilities, advertising customizable control and data sovereignty. The company has spent the last few weeks working with developers and leaders to assess the model’s cybersecurity capabilities, a practice that’s becoming commonplace for proprietary American labs like OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic as concerns about model security mounts.

Similarly to Anthropic’s Project Glasswing and OpenAI’s rollout of Astra, Mistral’s initial testing partners got access to a less guardrailed version of ML4 with “expanded cybersecurity capabilities.”

At least by some measure, ML4’s promises seem to have come true: Le Chonk scored just above DeepSeek V4.1 Flash on the CyberGym benchmark for defensive cybersecurity, which measures how well models find “real memory-safety vulnerabilities in C/C++ open-source projects, reproducing them with proof-of-concept inputs, and patching them without breaking the projects’ tests.”

Recent AI security incidents have somewhat pitted open and proprietary models against each other. Initially framed as less safe because of their malleability, open models are viewed as a new option for cyber defense after proprietary models from Anthropic and OpenAI proved just as risky.

Mistral said ML4 is built for security that stays under user control — unlike proprietary models, which frontier labs can technically rescind access to at any time.

“The cyber defense capabilities will enable enterprises and governments to defend themselves against threat actors that are jailbreaking closed models to perform cyberattacks,” Mistral co-founder Guillaume Lample said during a briefing for the Oct. 6 preview release.

Following the Hugging Face breach, Mistral was one of many companies that signed Nvidia’s Open Secure AI Alliance, a cross-industry partnership that argues open models are crucial to democratizing defenses against increasingly common AI security incidents.

**Also: This new ChatGPT scam tricks you into installing malware**

By Nvidia’s logic, and its Alliance that aims to democratize AI security tools, the race is between Mistral and other open models to achieve state-of-the-art security prowess.

## More for less compute

Training a competitive model in a compute shortage is no small task for a trimmer lab like Mistral, which doesn’t have the same resources as a pre-IPO giant like Anthropic.

**Also: These Claude Enterprise features let you track AI ROI**

“ML4 was trained from scratch on 4,000 Nvidia Grace Blackwell GPUs over two months, deployed in Mistral’s own data centers in Europe,” the company said. For context, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said on X that OpenAI trained GPT-6 Astra on roughly 100,000 GPUs.

title: SuperMe, which generates AI-powered chats with simulated profiles of prominent industry experts to let users ask questions, raised $20M

title_en: SuperMe, which generates AI-powered chats with simulated profiles of prominent industry experts to let users ask questions, raised $20M
excerpt_en: SuperMe, which generates AI-powered chats with simulated profiles of prominent industry experts to let users ask questions, raised $20M
content_en:
When people have career or job questions, they usually tap into their network to find experts who’ve faced a similar predicament and can offer answers. Increasingly, that job is falling to AI.

SuperMe is a network of AI profiles built from the knowledge of real-life experts. When you ask a question, the platform determines which experts are best suited to answer and creates a group chat with their AI profiles.

To scale that network on both sides, meaning more users asking questions and more experts supplying knowledge, the startup announced today that it is raising $20 million in funding led by Kirsten Green at Forerunner, with participation from Greylock Partners.

Casey Winters and Ludo Antonov founded the startup in 2024. Both have experience at large consumer companies. Winters held exec roles at Grubhub, Pinterest, and Eventbrite and has advised companies like Airbnb and Canva part-time. Antonov was head of engineering at multiple startups, including Pinterest, Lyft, and Whatnot.

The two got connected when Winters was advising Whatnot. ChatGPT was becoming popular around the same time, and they decided to build a network business using AI.

“There are these hidden networks in Silicon Valley of who the best people are for niche skills. Our idea was: Could we make that network of who the absolute best people are more transparent, and could we take all of the key insights that are locked inside their heads and make them more readily available?” Winters told TechCrunch over a call.

Users can go to the SuperMe website and type their question into the chatbot to start a group of experts. They can also return to a group they have formed or joined and ask follow-up questions.

You can ask a question like “Analyze my pitch deck. Which parts of the story are the weakest,

and which questions should I be most prepared to answer?” and get answers from AI profiles of longtime VCs like Mercedes Bent, Sarah Tavel, and Josh Elman. Users can also go to these people’s profiles and ask questions directly rather than in a group chat.

To collect knowledge from users, SuperMe scans public sources such as LinkedIn, YouTube, Substack, and blogs. It also draws on connected apps such as Google Drive, Notion, Gmail, and meeting notetaking tools like Granola. SuperMe said some of this data will include personal information and trade secrets, but it makes sure that none of it appears in answers.

The network is currently free, but the startup plans to cap the number of questions users can ask, after which they will have to cough up some money. It is also considering how to give experts incentives to add more knowledge.

SuperMe also works with MCP (Model Context Protocol, a standard that lets AI chatbots connect to outside tools and data), so users can ask questions from within chatbots such as Claude and ChatGPT.

The startup has about 13 employees. It is hiring on the tech side to improve its AI models for conversation and for matching questions to experts, and on the network side for someone to find experts in subject areas the platform doesn’t yet cover.

Forerunner’s Green said that SuperMe is well positioned to build a platform where AI collaborates with humans.

“I think it’s one of the reasons why this is very timely, and it’s good to have something like this establishing itself when we’re relatively early in this journey,” she told TechCrunch over a call. “Because there’s going to be so many lessons that are going to be learned, and they need to be shared so that people can come along in a productive way. I think that the balance here is to build a network so that you do have a true sharing component where there are incentives and benefits for everybody to contribute what they know.”

title_en: Wabi, the AI agent that builds mini apps, now valued at $1.25B after latest round
excerpt_en: On Thursday, AI app Wabi, now describing itself as a "personal agent," said it has raised $55 million at a $1.25 billion valuation.
content_en:
The race to build the winning AI assistant is on, and investors are spreading out their bets. On Thursday, another AI app, Wabi, now describing itself as a “personal agent,” said it has raised $55 million at a $1.25 billion valuation.

Founded by Eugenia Kuyda, who previously founded the AI companion startup Replika, Wabi originally focused on allowing anyone to build apps using prompts. Last month, however, the startup announced a pivot of sorts to become an AI messenger.

The idea now is that the new Wabi — or Wabi 2.0, as it was called — could build the interfaces you need to get things done as part of its role as your personal AI agent.

The company suggests Wabi could be used to build mini apps for things like meal planning, tracking local restaurants, planning date nights, creating fitness plans, designing specialized trivia games, and more.

The additional funding indicates that Wabi’s investors agree that its new agentic angle has some potential, especially given the market around AI agents is hot right now, with viral AI agent Instinct pulling in another billion at a $10 billion valuation in September.

Even Tolan, which makes a cute, Muppet-like AI companion to help people navigate life, just raised $30 million.

“Eugenia has a unique sense for where AI is headed and a track record of great taste in building it,” said Alex Lim, general partner at IVP, which led the new round, in a statement. “She has a clear vision for how people will interact with AI, one that goes far beyond the text box or command line. Wabi is the expression of that vision, and we’re thrilled to support her.”

Other participants in the round included Andreessen Horowitz (a16z), Forerunner, Amazon Alexa Fund, and angel investors like Shopify CEO Tobi Lütke, Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff, former Yahoo! head Marissa Mayer, former Twitter CEO Dick Costolo, and one half of The Chainsmokers, Alex Pall.

title: Mistral releases weights for its trillion-parameter AI model, targeting cybersecurity
excerpt: Mistral says its new model can afford organizations a kind of control over its cyber defenses that closed models can't.
title_en: Mistral releases weights for its trillion-parameter AI model, targeting cybersecurity
excerpt_en: Mistral says its new model can afford organizations a kind of control over its cyber defenses that closed models can't.
content_en:
French AI company Mistral has released the weights for its trillion-parameter open source AI model Mistral Large 4 (ML4), allowing businesses and governments to download and deploy the system themselves. Nicknamed “Le Chonk,” the model was first introduced earlier this month.

The release comes as competition between open-weight AI developers like Mistral and closed-model providers like OpenAI and Anthropic heats up, with the former arguing that businesses and governments shouldn’t have to rely on outside AI companies for access to advanced capabilities. That argument may hold more weight in cybersecurity, where organizations want more control over their data and systems.

Or, as Mistral’s CEO, Arthur Mensch, explained, AI should “be a tool for empowerment, not dominance.” With Chonk, Mistral doubles down on that position, arguing that it’s able to achieve “state-of-the-art performance” at a “fraction of the compute and capital committed by closed labs.”

The release of the model’s weights — the numerical training that animates the system — ensures that other companies and government agencies will now be able to deploy ML4 for their own purposes.

Mistral says that its model is comparable in terms of performance with a Chinese open-weight competitor, GLM-5.3, which was previously considered one of the best open-weight models in the world — particularly when it comes to cyber work. However, Mistral’s model uses 47 percent fewer tokens per task, making it significantly more economical than GLM-5.3.

The company also claims that the model outranks all other open models when it comes to agentic coding tasks on Artificial Analysis’ Coding Agent Index, an AI benchmarking site.

“Amid growing cyber threats, ML4 brings state-of-the-art sovereign cyber defense capabilities to enterprises and governments globally,” the company said Thursday. “Enterprise and public sector institutions can now download, deploy, and own frontier AI to detect, analyze, and respond to threats across code and IT infrastructure.”

The weights for ML4 are being made available on Hugging Face and via its API.

Pierre Stock, Vice President of Science at Mistral, told TechCrunch that the release of the model’s weights meant that organizations will have more control over how they use AI to defend themselves.

“Concretely, it means that, for instance, as a business company or as a government, you’re able to have access to frontier intelligence to defend yourselves against cyberattacks. Access that can’t be cut off by definition because the model is open-weighted,” he said.

Stock added that the model could be used to “identify, coordinate, and respond in real time to major security incidents, and that the open sourcing means that companies can deploy this model on-prem in their own ecosystem.

While advances in AI cybersecurity are helping security professionals to find bugs at a much higher rate than before, Stock continued, he believes it’s important for companies to “provide \[this same\] capability to everyone…as soon as possible to ramp up and to strengthen the ecosystem,” given that “some malicious actors might try to actually leverage their own technology to attack.”

Separately, Stock addressed concerns about recent incidents involving rogue AI agents, acknowledging the risks but cautioning against overreacting.

“We don’t want to fearmonger people. We think it’s a problem that is solvable. It’s a hard problem to have good security,” he said.

content_en:
Turning a simulation idea into a working application means assembling assets, connecting physics and rendering, and checking that the scene behaves as intended. Developers are combining frontier AI models with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to help carry out that work — building applications for exploring scenarios, investigating failures and improving designs.

Developers direct AI agents through natural-language instructions, review results and guide changes. Omniverse libraries provide GPU-accelerated physics, rendering and sensor simulation capabilities.

Explore the projects below to see frontier AI models such as GPT-6 Astra at work, and check back for new examples from NVIDIA teams and developers across the ecosystem.

## **Create an Editable Building Model From Site Scans 🔗**


Planning warehouse automation requires a model of the building itself, but shelving and machinery can obscure its structure in site scans. Omniverse brings together real-to-sim tools and agent skills to help developers turn real-world captures into editable starting environments for physical AI simulation.

David Wehr, from NVIDIA’s simulation technology team, built on that work using Astra to develop a workflow for digitally reconstructing a building without its contents. The goal is an editable, simulation-ready building model where developers can add or reposition shelving and machinery to evaluate warehouse layouts and automation plans before making physical changes.

Wehr guided Astra to interpret panoramic photos, create building geometry and align it with point-cloud measurements. OpenUSD stores the models, while Omniverse’s ovrtx library renders results for inspection.

## **Test Gas-Turbine Operating Scenarios With a Digital Twin 🔗**

# Paris-based Mistral releases "Le Chonk," a strong coding model that still trails China overall

## Key Points

- Mistral has released the weights for Large 4 ("Le Chonk"). The model has about one trillion parameters, 52 billion of them active, and can run on your own hardware under a modified MIT license.
- In independent benchmarks, the model does well on coding. On Artificial Analysis' Intelligence Index, though, it scores 26 points, behind open Chinese models like DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and GLM-5.3 and far behind the leading systems from Anthropic and Google.
- Its strengths are speed at 161 tokens per second, lower API prices, and a 96.6 percent refusal rate for harmful cyber requests.

**Mistral has released the weights for Mistral Large 4, its largest model yet. The company says the model beats its open rivals at coding. In the first independent test, it turns out to be fast and fairly cheap, but it trails Chinese models in the overall rankings.**

Three weeks after the public preview, Mistral has put the Large 4 weights on Hugging Face. The model's nickname is "Le Chonk." It takes text and images as input and outputs text and code. It has about one trillion parameters in total, with 52 billion active per step. Running it yourself takes a lot of hardware. According to the docs for the inference framework SGLang, the standard version runs on eight Nvidia B300 GPUs, and a more heavily compressed variant runs on four GB300 GPUs.

Since the preview, Mistral has kept training the model with reinforcement learning. The company says this brought big gains, especially in coding and cyber defense. Mistral researchers Pierre Stock and Corentin Petit walked through the process on a press call. The team built tasks in-house that got harder as training went on. They said the only limit on performance is how difficult a task the team can still create and verify. Mistral calls it a "two-year bet" that's now paying off.

## Large 4 leads open models on coding but trails Claude by a wide margin

After three more weeks of training, Large 4's score on Terminal-Bench 4.0 rose from 28 to 41 percent. That puts it just ahead of GLM-5.3 at 40 percent. Mistral says Large 4 hits 48 percent on Artificial Analysis' Coding Agent Index. That's practically tied with GLM-5.3, but Large 4 uses 47 percent fewer tokens to get there. Claude Code with Claude Opus 5.5 tops the index at 62 points.

On Cognition's new FrontierCode 2.0 benchmark, Large 4 leads the open models at 19.7 percent. Claude Opus 5.5, however, scores 46 percent. In blind comparisons run by Surge, testers preferred Large 4's code over code from GLM-5.3, Kimi K3, and DeepSeek more often than not. Against Opus 5.5, Large 4 won only 22 percent of matchups.

Mistral's comparisons leave out Moonshot's Kimi K3.1 Pro. Technically that's fair, since its weights aren't public yet. Moonshot plans to release them by November 4, 2026. After that, Mistral probably won't have much of a lead left, because Kimi K3.1 Pro tops Terminal-Bench 4.0 at 67 percent.

## Large 4 ranks third among open models in cyber defense, not first

Mistral calls Large 4 the leading open model for cyber defense. The company says the final version scores 51 percent on Artificial Analysis' Cyber Index. The index measures whether a model can find, reproduce, and patch security holes in a codebase without breaking existing features. Mistral's own chart, however, shows two open models ahead of it, with DeepSeek V4.1 Flash at 57 percent and MiMo-V2.6-Pro at 56 percent. That puts Large 4 third among open models, just ahead of GLM-5.3 Flash at 50 percent. Kimi K3.1 Pro leads the entire index at 64 percent.

The extra training barely moved the needle here. According to Artificial Analysis, the preview scored 50 points, and the final version is only one point higher.

Large 4 does better at refusing harmful requests. Mistral says it rejects 96.6 percent of malicious cyber requests on average, more than any other open model. It's still supposed to handle legitimate defensive tasks. Mistral admits the model could make real attacks easier, though, so it plans to tighten safeguards in the coming months. Select partners like Orange Cyberdefense are already testing a special version for penetration testing. Access requires a review and comes with contractual restrictions.

Mistral also sees progress on office work. The company says Large 4 trails only Kimi K3 among open models at editing financial spreadsheets and searching the web.

## Mistral cuts the price but adds a license catch

Through the API, Large 4 costs $0.70 per million input tokens and $2.10 per million output tokens. During the preview, the list price was $1.36 and $4.18. Mistral cut it to $0.68 and $2.09 for two weeks at launch, so the new price roughly matches that old discount. For comparison, Kimi K3.1 Pro costs $2 for input and $10 for output.

Mistral released the model under a modified MIT license. Use, modification, and commercial deployment are free. Companies that offer Large 4 as a commercial cloud service, however, need a separate license from Mistral. The company mainly pitches the model as "sovereign" AI, since it was trained entirely in Europe and can run on your own servers. If you don't want to host it yourself, it's available on Microsoft Foundry, among other platforms.

## Independent tests show Large 4 is fast and cheap but can't catch China's best

Artificial Analysis released version 5 of its Intelligence Index on Wednesday. It has since rated the final version of Large 4 in high mode, which scores 26 points. Three-fifths of the index now rely on tests whose tasks or solutions aren't public. The nine tests include Terminal-Bench 4.0 and FrontierCode 2.0.

The preview scored 25 points, so the three extra weeks of training added just one point overall. Artificial Analysis says Large 4 beats the average for open models of similar size, where the median is 23 points. It still falls short of the strongest open models from China. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and GLM-5.3 each score 32 points, and MiMo-V2.6-Pro gets 30. That gap isn't new. In the old index, the preview scored 38 points and GLM-5.3 scored 45.

Large 4's strengths are speed and cost. The model generates 161 tokens per second, up from 111 for the preview. In Artificial Analysis' head-to-head comparison, only DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and Muse Wonder are faster. An index task costs $2.06 on average with Large 4, down from $5.54 for the preview. That makes Large 4 cheaper than GLM-5.3 ($5.01) and Kimi K3.1 Pro ($3.68), but much more expensive than DeepSeek V4.1 Flash ($0.60) and MiMo-V2.6-Pro ($0.26). Compared with other open models of similar size, Artificial Analysis still considers its per-token price on the high side.

Mistral also promises that Large 4 is efficient with tokens, and that claim can now be checked. The model generated 110 million output tokens across the full index, compared with 150 million for the preview. That's a big improvement. But the median for comparable models is 100 million, so Large 4 still sits slightly above it.

The gap at the top of the index is wide. Google's Gemini 4 Carbon leads with 59 points, one point ahead of Claude Opus 5.5. So far, though, only select cybersecurity partners can use Gemini 4 Carbon. The top open model is Kimi K3.1 Pro at 46 points, but its weights haven't been released yet.

Mistral still thinks it's on track. The team said on the press call that it works with a fraction of the resources US and Chinese labs have and would be at the top with ten times more capital. Large 4 is meant to serve as the base for specialized Mistral models. The company wouldn't comment yet on smaller versions built on it.

### Mistral releases open weights for Mistral Large 4, providing sovereign control for the company’s ‘Le Chonk’ AI model

Mistral AI SAS today announced the availability of the open weights of its frontier model Mistral Large 4, nicknamed “Le Chonk,” the company’s most capable large language model to date, initially released in preview three weeks ago.

With 1 trillion parameters and 52 billion active parameters, ML4 is natively multimodal and has received three additional weeks of reinforcement training and customer testing. The company says it’s becoming one of the best open agentic coding models in the world, offering leading performance at a small fraction of the token cost with state-of-the-art cyber defense capabilities.

“ML4 OSS showcases our science team’s ability to innovate at speed,” said Vice President of Science Pierre Stock. “Building on the ML4 Preview, the open-weight version continues reinforcement learning training and delivers substantial gains with no signs of saturation.”

The company trained ML4 on 3,800 Nvidia Corp. Grace Blackwell graphics processing units in its European data centers to achieve high-fidelity performance for tool use and coding, driven by end-to-end control of its infrastructure and the ability to optimize for hardware during model development.

Open weights mean companies can take the model and deploy it on their own hardware, within their own firewalls, and run sensitive data without exposing it to the cloud or outside parties. With Mistral’s model, companies will have a Western-developed model to compete with the multitude of ultra-large Chinese coding models on the market, such as the GLM family from Beijing Zhipu Huazhang Technology Co. Ltd. and the Kimi family from Beijing Moonshot AI Technology Co. Ltd.

“Open source is essential to ensure state-of-the-art AI does not end up concentrated in the hands of a few actors,” said co-founder and Chief Executive Arthur Mensch. “Other labs have raised hundreds of billions to develop equivalent capabilities; in three years, Mistral raised roughly $6 billion.”

Because of its training regimen, ML4 stands out among many other frontier models, rivaling even top models such as Chinese-built GLM-5.3 on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index while using 47% fewer tokens per task on average.

On Terminal-Bench 4.0, which tests agentic coding in the terminal, ML4 climbed from 28% to 41%, tying GLM-5.3 as the best model for coding agents.

Mistral offers three reasoning modes for ML4: low, medium and high. Teams can use this to match reasoning depth to the task without adjusting prompts, which can be less effective, allowing reasoning to fit quick everyday tasks to deep work on extremely complex problems. This allows developers and enterprise users to control token use per task.

The company said the release of ML4 represents a new generation of Mistral models spanning all modalities. It follows the recent launch of Voxtral 3, a family of voice models and voice agents. Mistral plans to continue to release additional models from this family in the coming months.

title_en: Mistral Says Its AI Model ‘Le Chonk’ Has Leapfrogged China in the Open-Weight Race
excerpt_en: The French AI lab claims its latest release matches or outperforms even the best models from DeepSeek and Z.ai in coding and cybersecurity.
content_en:
A few weeks ago, French company Mistral released an early version of its new artificial intelligence model, nicknamed Le Chonk. At the time, the company said it was the most advanced open-weight offering outside of China. After further refinement, Mistral now says Le Chonk is the “world’s best” open-weight model for automated coding and cybersecurity.

The advances, Mistral says, were made possible by feeding the model increasingly difficult cybersecurity and coding problems, which allowed the trillion-parameter Le Chonk to match or surpass models from leading Chinese labs like DeepSeek and Z.ai.

“It’s a pivotal moment in the global AI leadership race,” Pierre Stock, VP of science at Mistral, told reporters during a press briefing. “It offers frontier capabilities for enterprises and governments to defend against an increasing threat level in cyber.”

The finalized version of Le Chonk is now freely available for anybody to access. After a flurry of AI-related cybersecurity incidents, Mistral claims that it’s important for the West to have its own advanced open-weight models. “You have no guarantee that \[Chinese models\] won’t behave maliciously. They can be threat vectors,” Stock said.

The most high-profile episode occurred when one of OpenAI’s models broke loose from a testing sandbox and hacked into multiple companies over the summer. It sparked panic over the idea that AI could escape human oversight and be abused by threat actors to launch sophisticated cyberattacks. (One of the affected companies, Hugging Face, used an open-weight model from China to assess and defend against the attack.)

Since then, AI has unearthed security vulnerabilities in ubiquitous software, too. In October, a raft of websites were taken offline after an AI tool discovered serious flaws in a foundational piece of web technology.

Mistral pitches its open-weight models, like Le Chonk, as part of the solution. If AI is destined to become a central feature of both cyber offense and defense, the argument goes, businesses and governments will need to be equipped with models that are freely available and cannot be switched off remotely, unlike proprietary models from the likes of OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google.

“AI is going to be like electricity. You don’t want to live in a world in which your neighbor can cut off electricity from one day to another,” Stock said. “Once you open source the weights, they’re all over the internet. It’s impossible to cut off access.”

The trade-off, however, is that freely available models can also be downloaded and customized by threat actors.

“It’s clearly a dual-use technology,” Rafe Pilling, senior director of threat intelligence at security company Sophos, tells WIRED. “Anything that’s available to download and circulate unfettered has the ability to be abused as well as used for productive purposes.”

According to Pilling, though it’s possible a Chinese model with internet access could siphon away data, all advanced models are capable of going rogue without careful supervision—no matter their country of origin.

“The technical realities and the narrative—which often has a nationalistic leaning—are two different things,” he says.“It’s about having the right monitoring and controls in place to be confident that, even if the model was trying to be deceptive or nefarious, you might have some way of detecting it.”
