title_en: How we detect frontier model misalignment
excerpt_en: OpenAI uses layered monitoring to detect frontier model misalignment and unauthorized agent behavior so responders can intervene before incidents escalate.
content_en:
# How we detect frontier model misalignment

As we train increasingly capable AI models, we need reliable ways to detect when their behavior departs from what we intended. Agents can misbehave and take unauthorized actions during training, evaluation, or deployment, with potentially serious consequences. In order to detect these failures—and, where necessary, to intervene in time—we monitor how agents reason, what actions they take, and how those actions affect their environment.

While we’ve been <u>monitoring our internal coding agents</u> for some time, the <u>Hugging Face incident</u> exposed a gap in our coverage: the incident began during internal cybersecurity evaluations on which we were not running our monitors for misaligned behavior. In response to that incident, and to the <u>increasing capabilities</u> of our models more generally, we’ve substantially expanded our system for monitoring agents’ behavior. Our misalignment monitors now cover our frontier models across a much wider variety of surfaces, including training, evaluation, internal use, and, with modifications depending on the product surface, external deployment.

In order to see how this expanded system could have helped prevent the Hugging Face incident, we replayed the behavior recorded in that episode with our strengthened monitors in place. In that simulation, our monitoring system alerted our security team about 30 minutes after the agents first escaped their sandbox—and more than 30 hours before Hugging Face’s systems were breached in the actual incident. We believe that this warning would have given our responders time to interrupt the activity well before our models were able to access external services.

In September, we saw how responders used an alert during a live training run. A model found a way to <u>reach the internet</u>(opens in a new window) from an environment that was meant to be isolated. Our monitors flagged the breach within 15 minutes, and a responder began reviewing it three minutes later. We then paused frontier reinforcement learning while we strengthened the systems that contain our agents.

While this monitoring system demands substantial compute, we think that cost is worth paying as our models become more capable and the potential consequences of model misalignment increase. Monitoring is one of several layers in our strategy of <u>defense in depth</u> against harm from misaligned model behavior. Alignment training aims to reduce models’ propensities toward harmful behavior; security controls <u>limit the systems an agent can access or affect</u>; and, when those safeguards fail, monitoring helps us detect the failures that remain, intervene before harm occurs, and learn from what went wrong. We believe that <u>all model developers</u> should monitor the behavior of their most capable models.

Below, we describe how our internal monitoring system works, what it has found so far, and how we’re evaluating and improving its performance.

For models at least as capable as GPT‑6 Astra, we monitor every reinforcement learning (RL) run and evaluation, as well as any harness that supports tool use. For most workloads, including RL and evaluations, we also monitor models we assess to be more capable than GPT‑5.5 Thinking. We also monitor all internal Codex traffic, regardless of the model being used. A version of this system also monitors external tool use for models above the Critical threshold for cybersecurity capabilities under our <u>Preparedness Framework</u>, as described below in this post.

In order to detect incidents while using compute efficiently, we’ve designed our monitoring system to follow a multilayer architecture. We spend relatively little compute on the first screening stages, where we want to catch as many concerning cases as we can: those stages are designed to pass cases along, even when the evidence is ambiguous. Later stages can spend more compute on each case to work out what happened, whether the model’s behavior is concerning, and whether we need to intervene.

Our initial layer (L0) uses lightweight classifiers we call *activation probes*. They look for concerning patterns in the model’s internal activations, and pass flagged cases to the next layer for review. We tune these probes for high recall, accepting some false alarms to reduce the chance of missing concerning behavior.

Because we’re still evaluating how well the probes detect unfamiliar forms of misalignment, we also send the next layer a random 5 percent of the traffic that our probes don’t flag. Reviewing that sample helps us identify concerning behavior the probes may have missed. Because of their sensitivity, we have our frontier RL runs and internal Codex traffic skip this layer and proceed directly to the next one.

At the next layer (L1), a model-based reviewer examines the agent’s recent conversation, chain of thought, and tool use. It looks for signs of deception, unauthorized actions, and attempts to manipulate an evaluation. The reviewer does this using the same context window the agent had when it acted. If the agent’s earlier work has been summarized for the context window under review, the reviewer sees that summary.

For frontier RL runs and internal Codex traffic, we run an L1 check at the end of each turn and whenever the agent summarizes its earlier work to make room in its context window. We are now moving to a schedule with no more than 30 minutes between these checks.

An agent’s actions can look quite different once we know what it was asked to do. When the L1 reviewer flags a case, it’s sent to our next layer (L2) for further inspection by our investigative agent. This investigative agent can check the purpose of an evaluation and, where the full transcript is available, read back across all of the agent’s context windows to see how it arrived at its actions. The investigative agent can also write and run code in an isolated environment to examine the relevant evidence. It then uses what it finds to reconstruct the incident, identify duplicate reports, and make a decision about how serious the case is.

We use different investigative agents for different purposes. Our security investigator looks for signs that someone may need to intervene—such as when an agent escaped its sandbox or accessed a system without authorization. Our alignment investigator, meanwhile, looks for behavior worth studying even when it poses no immediate security risk. Where both investigators are in use, each reviews every case flagged by our L1 layer. We are currently expanding the use of alignment investigations across our internal workloads.

For sensitive workloads, including internal Codex use, evaluations, and RL runs, a further check at our next layer (L3) draws on evidence outside the conversation. The security investigator compares the transcript with network logs, other system telemetry, and evidence from earlier cases to decide whether to alert a human responder. At L3, alignment reviewers also compare reports across cases to identify serious failures and recurring patterns, and examine frontier RL runs in greater depth.

For workloads that skip this layer, the L2 security investigator can alert responders directly.

When paging is enabled, the highest-priority security alerts reach members of our security and training teams, typically within 15 minutes of the initial alert. Responders review the evidence, examine the affected systems, and take action to contain the incident. How we follow up on less urgent findings, such as alignment failures that don’t pose immediate security risks, depends on the relevant workload.

False alarms have made it difficult to keep paging enabled around the clock for every workload. For frontier RL runs, a highest-priority alert can page a human responder at any hour. title_en: Ex-Palantir execs launch Dream with $17M from a16z to build AI world models for construction
excerpt_en: Dream is grounded in real physics and construction standards. Just as LLMs learn from text, Dream's world model is trained on more than 100 million square feet of building data gathered from permit archives across the United States.
content_en:
Andy Elder and Arjun Mathur were Stanford roommates who both studied computer science before spending a decade at Palantir. Elder led product design for a team of 800 people building software for U.S. defense and intelligence agencies, while Mathur served as a senior vice president in the company’s commercial practice. When the friends decided to build a startup early last year, there was no question they would do it together.

Despite having no direct background in architecture, Elder and Mathur were troubled by a growing problem: Fewer buildings are constructed in the U.S. today than a few decades ago, as development costs have surged.

“We’ve gone from dial-up internet to superintelligent AI, but our ability to build the physical world around us has actually decreased,” Mathur told TechCrunch.

Believing AI can boost productivity across the architecture, engineering, and construction (AEC) industry, they set out to build Dream, a startup developing built world models that automate building design and engineering. Dream has emerged from stealth with $17 million in seed funding led by Andreessen Horowitz, alongside other backers, including SV Angel, XYZ, and Zigg Capital. The startup aims to replace cumbersome, outdated AEC tools like Autodesk’s AutoCAD and Revit.

If you sit next to an architect or a structural engineer, you’ll notice that they are still “drawing” every piece of their designs part by part on legacy software, Mathur said. “AI really plays no role in that equation.”

While a standard LLM like ChatGPT can generate an image of a building, the result won’t be structurally sound. Dream, by contrast, is grounded in real physics and construction standards. Just as LLMs learn from text, Dream’s world model is trained on more than 100 million square feet of building data gathered from permit archives across the United States.

“Our model actually understands what’s within those walls. What materials are used, what the beams are made of, and how much weight they can support,” Elder said.

The startup calls its approach “structural cognition” because its model generates structurally precise designs that account for internal building elements like plumbing and HVAC.

Dream has already begun selling its product to AEC professionals and developers, who use the model to conceptualize building designs and estimate overall costs, according to the founders. The platform is already deployed across 10 active projects in Texas and California.

While Dream isn’t the only company attempting to update AEC software with AI — other startups working on this include Motif, Snaptrude, and Arcol — Elder and Mathur claim that they are the only ones that developed a world model that instantly designs whole buildings.

Kimberly Tan, a partner at Andreessen Horowitz, said that while the firm first invested in Dream over a year ago, when the startup model was just an idea, she has been extremely impressed with their progress. “I have not seen anybody take the technical approach,” she said. “They’re doing everything based on their own models.”

content_en:
Meta has quietly launched Style Sketch, an AI fashion app that helps users put together outfit ideas using clothes they already own. The app connects to Instagram to build a virtual closet from photos you’ve posted, or lets you add items manually by snapping a photo, recording a quick video, or uploading images from your camera roll.

Style Sketch then suggests outfit combinations built from your wardrobe matched to your style. Users can then try on the outfits on a “realistic model matched to your body shape and skin tone,” the app description reads.

The app, which was first spotted by social media consultant Matt Navarra, is available in Indonesia, Singapore, and Thailand on iOS and Android.

Meta did not respond to TechCrunch’s request for comment. It’s unknown whether Meta plans to launch Style Sketch more widely.

Several apps already use AI to help users digitize their wardrobes and visualize new outfits, including startups like Alta. Even Google Photos offers tools that let users turn photos of their clothes into digital closets where they can create new outfit ideas.

To compete with what’s already on the market, Meta will likely rely less on the novelty of the idea and more on the app’s integration with Instagram, where users already have a visual record of their personal style.

Rather than relying on random suggestions, users can also select a specific item from their wardrobe and get fresh outfit ideas built around it, according to the app description.

The app can also help users plan outfits for trips. If they enter their destination, trip length and planned activities, users can get a day-by-day outfit plan that takes the weather forecast and itinerary into account.

Style Sketch is one of many AI apps from Meta in recent months. Most recently, the company launched an app called Waddle World, which essentially looks like a Tamagotchi clone, but with AI. Meta has also launched Pocket, a tool for vibe-coding games, and Vibes, which lets users quickly generate AI-powered videos.

The wave of new apps is part of a broader effort at Meta to release more apps. The Wall Street Journal reported earlier this year that CEO Mark Zuckerberg told employees the company plans to release far more apps than it has historically, as AI-driven efficiencies have made it faster and easier to ship new apps.

content_en:
A top executive of a Singapore AI cloud firm that was accused of illegally selling Nvidia chips to China could also have been a Chinese spy, anonymous sources told the New York Times.

The executive, Alice Huang (or Huang Le), worked for Megaspeed and was photographed as one of multiple people hanging out with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang during various business dinners in the Singapore region. U.S. intelligence agencies had been surveilling Alice Huang to learn more about her ties with China for about a year, the Times reports.

The concern, sources said, was that Alice Huang had grown so close to Jensen Huang that she could have been gathering information about Nvidia’s plans and the CEO’s efforts to convince the Trump administration to allow it to ship more advanced technology to China.

But an Nvidia spokesperson denied this, telling TechCrunch that the CEO’s relationship with the Megaspeed executive was the same as with any other regional customer.

“Jensen’s interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a C.E.O.’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year,” the spokesperson said in an emailed statement. The company also said, “Our regional cloud customers receive ordinary business information — not sensitive NVIDIA trade secrets — and zero information relevant to national security.”

In 2025, the Times reported that the Commerce Department had investigated Megaspeed over concerns that it was helping Chinese companies sidestep AI chip export regulations by reselling restricted chips to them. Alice Huang was said to be a top executive for the firm at the time.

content_en:
**Bleu Robotics**, a Paris-based startup building AI models for industrial humanoid robots, has raised a €5 million pre-Seed round, to reach its goal of reducing the full humanoid robot deployment process to one hour or shorter.

The round was co-led by Contrarian Ventures and OVNI Capital, with participation from Kvanted, WEPA Ventures, Motier Ventures and Charlie Songhurst, and board members at Meta.

**Benoît Berkoukchi**, co-founder of Bleu Robotics, says, “*Humanoid robots in manufacturing are the next automotive sector, with the potential to help Europe and the US reshore production. But most robotics companies are trying to train humanoids with millions of data points and build fully general-purpose models. That approach isn’t suited to manufacturing. There isn’t enough data on factory work, and there won’t be internet-scale data, the kind LLMs were built on, for robots for a long time. Our methodology means we can do more with less*.”

The round comes amid continued European investment in robotics software, humanoid systems and Physical AI during 2026.

In France, Paris-based Inbolt raised €11 million to expand its hardware-agnostic robot intelligence platform, while Norway- and US-based Trener Robotics secured €26 million to develop AI-powered skills for industrial robots.

Elsewhere, Belgium’s Motion raised €1.7 million for humanoid deployment, Spain’s THEKER secured €73 million to scale generalist industrial robotics, and London-based Humanoid raised €133 million for its industrial humanoid platform.

Together with funding rounds for Germany’s Sereact, Switzerland’s Enact Intelligence and Poland’s Nomagic, these financings total €372.7 million in 2026, rising to €377.7 million when including Bleu Robotics’ latest round.

**Thomas Poitrineau**, Investor at Contrarian Ventures, adds, “*We were attracted to Bleu Robotics because of their ambitious choice to rethink how humanoid robotics software should work from first principles. It’s rare to find a company led by two world-class robotics researchers and a manufacturing expert, which is also why their software works differently from their competition. Their goal is far bigger than simply making the best model in a lab. It’s an approach that can already scale, putting robots to work in factories within months rather than years*.”

Founded in Paris in 2025 by two INRIA researchers and a former Renault manufacturing manager, Bleu’s abductive learning technology reportedly lets robots learn new tasks from only a handful of operator demonstrations.

Its software runs on any humanoid platform and includes the AI model and training devices needed to teach robots on the factory floor.

According to the International Federation of Robotics, there were 5 million industrial robots operating globally in 2025. However, these robots are built to repeat fixed tasks, and are unable to adapt to the high-mix, low-volume production now common in modern manufacturing, so that work still falls to human workers.

Humanoid robots are needed to automate a wider range of complex tasks. While hardware has advanced significantly in recent years, software development has struggled to keep pace, limiting real-world deployment.

Interact Analysis found that of the 20,000-plus humanoids produced last year, only 10% reached real-world applications. Most of these robots today rely on end-to-end models, which learn everything in a single black box and require massive amounts of data to achieve production-ready reliability.

As a result, deployment remains costly and time-consuming for manufacturers, often requiring hundreds of hours of training data, with no guarantee the robot will perform reliably.

Instead of an end-to-end model, Bleu Robotics’ abductive learning model allows the robot to learn a new task from as few as ten operator demonstrations, while keeping the explainability required for industrial safety and the 99%+ accuracy that production lines demand.

### Motion Picture Association runs its legal operations on a CRM built for sales

Legal operations teams are finding that software built for sales pipelines can just as easily run investigations and member communications. As AI agents take on triage work, even nontechnical teams are building those workflows themselves.

That shift is playing out at the Motion Picture Association Inc., where a CRM module on monday.com Ltd.’s AI work platform now anchors piracy investigations and content protection cases. It links offices in Asia-Pacific, Europe, Latin America, Canada and the U.S., according to Melisa King (pictured), legal operations administrator and senior paralegal at the MPA.

“We have a lot of players in the kitchen, and the CRM module helps us communicate not just internally but externally,” King said. “So our members can have real-time information, find out what’s missing, if there’s documents they need to sign, and it really just helps us move the beast.”

King spoke with Rebecca Knight at monday.com’s Elevate event, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how the MPA tracks anti-piracy cases, how an AI agent triages security alerts and why CRM isn’t just for sales. *(\* Disclosure below.)*

### AI triage lightens the legal operations load

Every case starts with a person. A tip comes in, an investigator checks it and the case goes onto a board, where the team weighs a takedown, a cease-and-desist letter or litigation. Studio powers of attorney are tracked there too, so investigators know where they can act, King explained.

“I think before, each region really worked independently from one another, and this has allowed us to collaborate and work together,” she said.

The newest addition is an AI agent, the kind of tool monday.com is having every Elevate attendee build. It triages security advisories for the Trusted Partner Network, which vets editing bays, before a point person decides who needs a follow-up. King tested it before launch and built it without a coding background.

“I think with anyone, we get hundreds of emails a day and it’s really easy to ignore these alerts,” she said.

For a small legal operations team, the payoff is time, efficiency and analytics showing members how many cases were stopped before litigation. King’s advice to teams that see CRM as a sales-only tool is to think bigger.

“I would say to think of it as project management on steroids with the communication aspect tied to it,” King said. “The communication is key because it keeps everyone connected, especially when people are working remote or hybrid or around the world.”

Until earlier in the year, the play was around having a focused app that does one thing well. But now, all of these apps are thinking about how to get more out of capturing users’ speech.

content_en:
Swedish AI startup **Pixel Systems** has raised €2.7 million ($3.1 million) in a Seed round to accelerate their commercial initiatives and continue building the technology that helps identify AI-generated and manipulated images, documents, and other digital material.

The round was led by Unconventional Ventures, at a pre-money valuation of approximately €18 million ($21 million).

“*Generative AI has made it extremely cheap to fabricate evidence. The problem is that almost every digital process still rests on the assumption that what people submit is authentic. That assumption is disappearing,*” says **Robel Efrem**, co-founder and CEO of Pixel.

Pixel’s funding follows other European investments in digital trust and fraud-prevention technology reported by EU-Startups in 2026, including Sweden’s Bits (€12 million), Denmark’s Flare (€3.6 million), France’s Marble (€6.5 million) and MokN (€12.9 million), Spain’s Zepo Intelligence (€12.8 million), and UK/Germany-based Diligent AI (€2.1 million).

Together, these rounds represent approximately €49.9 million in funding, excluding Pixel’s €2.7 million Seed round, across companies addressing different aspects of verification, fraud prevention and financial crime.

EU-Startups previously covered Efrem as co-founder and CEO of Swedish esports platform Challengermode, which raised €10.1 million in 2020.

“*We believe the ability to verify digital information will become as natural a part of tomorrow’s infrastructure as cybersecurity is today. That a Swedish company has the opportunity to take a leading position in this field is exactly the kind of development we want to help make possible,*” adds **Nora Bavey**, General Partner at Unconventional Ventures.

Founded in 2026 in Stockholm, Pixel develops proprietary technology to detect AI-generated and manipulated digital content. By combining several independent forensic analysis methods, Pixel helps companies verify images, documents, and other digital material before it is used as the basis for decisions, payouts, or other critical processes.

The team behind Pixel consists of senior engineers, AI specialists, and competitive programmers.

In Pixel’s internal tests, the platform has achieved a detection rate of 99.98 percent for AI-generated and manipulated material, reportedly placing the technology at a world-leading level.

Pixel is used today in businesses where digital material forms the basis for financial decisions, including insurance, FinTech, e-commerce, and professional services.

Use cases include manipulated damage photos in insurance claims, fabricated receipts and invoices, AI-generated product images in refund fraud, and manipulated material in financial or legal processes.

“*The internet was built for a world where an image could largely be treated as proof. That world no longer exists. Now every company that receives images, receipts, and documents from its customers needs to be able to check that material before money is paid out,*” says **Robel Efrem**.

The funding comes just months after the company was founded. Three weeks after its commercial launch, Pixel has reached its first €89k ($100k) in contracted recurring revenue.

content_en:
*The New York Times* is testing a new AI feature for its Cooking app that helps users to modify recipes, and it has sparked some drama among users. Last Friday, *NYT* Cooking senior editor Genevieve Ko announced the feature, which can be used to recommend substitutions for ingredients and cooking equipment, scale recipes to any number of servings, and “generally make our recipes work for what a cook needs at that moment.”

# The NYT Cooking app is testing AI recipe modifications

Some users aren’t exactly thrilled with The New York Times’ recipe-tweaking AI tool.

One of the examples given in the article shows a user asking to use baby spinach instead of kale, with the Cooking app feature advising that because baby spinach wilts faster, it should be added during a later step of the recipe. Ko says it can also change the recipes around different pans and tools. Customized recipes are private and can’t be published or shared through the app. The AI modification feature is being rolled out gradually while the *NYT* monitors how it performs — it’s currently available to all Cooking subscribers on the iOS app, and it will be more broadly available “soon.”

Some *NYT* readers have pushed back against the feature, citing concerns in the article’s comment section around the environmental impact of widespread AI adoption and the general impact that AI features may have on the user experience. When one user asked if there will be a way to disable the AI feature, Ko responded with, “No, not at this time,” and noted that the feature is “completely optional to use.”

“Unbelievably disappointing to see,” said another *NYT* user. “I’ve always loved NYT Cooking and it pains me that the AI mandate has reached what used to be a wonderful and simple collection of recipes and notes from all sorts of different people.”

This isn’t the first time that AI has been used by the NYT Cooking app. Ko says it was used to convert imperial volume measurements to metric weight measurements in recipes two years ago, and a feature was added last year that converts recipes to halve or double the original serving size. The comments on the new AI feature announcement post have since been closed, but *NYT* spokesperson Jordan Cohen tells *The Verge* that this is standard practice:

“Comments on this article remained open for four days, with editors from Cooking taking care to answer questions, address concerns and engage directly with readers. We kept that conversation open to give readers a meaningful opportunity to share feedback and hear from the team. Closing comments on older articles is standard practice at The Times so that our moderators can focus on new discussions. We’re pleased to see that many members of our Cooking community are interested in exploring this tool and are already trying it out on our iOS app; they’re reporting good results.”

content_en:
Thrive Holdings has acquired physical security company ADT for $10 per share or about $7.6 billion in equity, the companies announced on Thursday. Beyond equity, the total enterprise value of the deal is $15.3 billion, ADT said.

Thrive Holdings is the PE spinout from Josh Kushner’s powerhouse VC firm Thrive Capital. It also counts OpenAI as its partner, as well as an investor. The firm’s mission is to hold other companies long-term, revitalizing them with AI. Currently, Thrive Holdings holds over 75 companies, it says.

As a partner, OpenAI supplies AI models and tech as well as people, otherwise known as forward-deployed engineers, to Thrive’s companies.

Neither ADT nor Thrive announced what new AI-powered security products they will be releasing, but they did tease that the plan was to invest and release new products. “ADT will form the foundation of Thrive Holdings’ smart home security business,” the press release said.

AI-powered physical security is having a moment right now. Apple just entered the field with a new line of smart home and home security products in collaboration with LG and Schneider Electric. Amazon updated its smart home line, including new AI-powered home cameras. And who knows what the future might bring? Some startups are offering AI dog robots as roving security guards.

Rivian is now licensing elements of its AI voice assistant technology to Volkswagen Group as part of the broader joint venture, according to the company’s third-quarter investor presentation released Thursday.

However, the AI assistant, which recently rolled out to Rivian vehicles, could make its Volkswagen debut in the automaker’s low-cost EV called the ID EVERY1. The small four-door hatchback is slated to be the first VW vehicle to use Rivian’s software and electrical architecture under the joint venture established in 2024.

The joint venture between Rivian and VW Group has already expanded once before, at least financially. The companies initially announced a joint venture valued up to $5 billion, but within months VW upped its commitment to invest up to $5.8 billion in Rivian by 2027. The initial tie-up, formalized through an independent company that kicked off in November 2024, focused on bringing Rivian’s electrical architecture and software to Volkswagen’s next generation of vehicles.

Rivian described the expansion to include elements of its AI assistant technology as “a proof point for the extensibility of the platform we’ve built in-house.”

Rivian spent two years developing its AI assistant before showing it off last year. That development work continued longer than expected, with the assistant finally rolling out in May 2026 to its flagship R1S SUV, R1T pickup truck, and in October to its new midsize R2 SUV.

Rivian has big aspirations for its AI assistant, which allows drivers and passengers to interact with the vehicle and control certain functions. Rivian founder and CEO RJ Scaringe told TechCrunch onstage at Disrupt 2026 that the company has created its own in-house agentic framework that understands what action a person wants to take when they talk to the vehicle, and routes it to the right part of the car’s software. That capability could eventually allow Rivian vehicles to run AI agents created by other companies, including Anthropic.

The in-house AI assistant program also fits into Rivian’s push to become more vertically integrated — a strategy the company emphasized in its third-quarter earnings report.

“Our relentless focus on vertical integration remains a core competitive differentiator, allowing Rivian to seamlessly unify our hardware and software architecture to deliver significant value to our customers,” the company noted in its investor presentation.

That strategy led to Rivian overhauling its flagship R1T truck and R1S SUV, changing everything from the battery pack and suspension system to the electrical architecture, sensor stack, and software user interface. Its new electric architecture system and compute platform slashed the amount of wiring used and reduced the total number of electronic control units, or computers, used to control the vehicle from 17 different ECUs to seven. That foundation, Rivian argued, would allow it to build vehicles that can handle the computing demands required for advanced software and automated driving.

That technology caught the attention (and money) of VW, which has struggled to offer customers a modern software-centric vehicle found in competitors like Tesla.

Rivian made that vertical-integration case repeatedly in its investor presentation, noting that because it controls the entire technology stack, including compute, sensors, displays, lighting, and sound, “it can roll out rapid, vehicle-wide OTA updates that go well beyond the basics.”

content_en:
# Experts adopt AI agent's random opinions and think they're their own, Anthropic study finds

## Key Points

- Anthropic had 50 experts use an AI agent to work through four analytical tasks with no clearly right answer. The agent's preference for one of two valid options was set by coin toss.
- Participants followed the agent's preference in up to 86 percent of cases, and most believed the final result was their own. Experience, expertise, and trust in AI made no difference. Participants did work faster and made fewer serious errors with AI.
- The authors warn that if many teams use the same model, they could create a false consensus in research and weaken AI safety checks. They suggest agents should argue both sides or ask users for their view first.

**An experiment by Anthropic with 50 experts found that people often followed their AI agent's randomly assigned preference on questions with no clearly right answer, and most thought the final result was their own.**

Handing a data analysis to an AI agent saves time and manual work, but it raises the question of who actually makes the decisions that shape the final recommendation. An Anthropic study suggests the agent makes most of them, often without the experts noticing.

In the experiment, 50 experts in causal inference worked on a realistic analysis task where they examined observational data from a fictional farming cooperative and estimated the productivity gains from a voluntary farm advisory program. They then had to recommend whether the cooperative should expand the program to all farms or end it, though participants or the agent could also suggest extending it for one year.

What participants didn't know was that a coin toss had set the agent's preference for one of two valid options at each decision point. The agent couldn't lie or hide data; it only had to make the strongest honest case for its assigned side.

## Experts followed the AI's view in up to 86 percent of cases

Participants adopted the agent's preference in 86 percent of the four analytical decisions, such as how to measure productivity or which statistical method to use. That's far above the 50 percent you'd expect if people chose at random. The authors call the agent's net influence the "flip rate," which ranged from 62 to 82 percent depending on the task.

Already having an opinion offered little protection. When participants made a choice before the agent stated its preference, an opposing view made them 53 percentage points more likely to switch sides than an agreeing one.

The authors tested possible safeguards, including years of analysis experience, self-rated expertise, education, test scores, and trust in AI. None had a statistically reliable link to the results after correcting for multiple tests. Age stood out before that correction, though the sample of 50 gave the study little power to detect such effects.

## Most experts thought the final call was their own

The agent's assigned preference had only a small direct effect on the final policy recommendation to the cooperative's board, slightly shifting votes without reaching statistical significance. Some experts even overruled the agent when its advice didn't match their calculated estimate of productivity.

That may sound reassuring, as though AI makes suggestions and people make decisions. But the researchers say the final result doesn't show that participants kept control. The four earlier analytical decisions had a major effect on the estimated productivity gain, which in turn shaped the board recommendation.

When asked afterward, 52 percent of participants said the recommendation felt more like their own than the agent's, and another 35 percent said it was mostly or entirely their own. Participants correctly recalled their choice for 85 percent of decisions, yet 77 percent, or 37 of 48, used at least one of the agent's arguments in their explanations, sometimes in nearly the same words. Only 15 percent mentioned AI at all.

The conversation logs show that the agent stated a position first in 77 percent of decisions. It then usually argued only for its preferred side, without explaining why skilled experts might choose the alternative, though it did explain how a different choice would affect the result, according to the paper.

Participants also worked much faster and made fewer errors with AI. Without an agent, 55 percent of analyses, or 6 of 11, had serious methodological or coding flaws, and the median time was 90 minutes. With AI, just 6 percent, or 3 of 50 analyses, had serious flaws, and participants finished in 65 minutes. The small group that worked without AI had chosen not to use the tool and had somewhat less expertise, so the researchers can't say for sure how much of the gap came directly from AI.

## False consensus and weaker safety checks

The researchers say this quiet deference could have wide effects in science. If many research teams use the same model with fixed default preferences, they could end up creating a false consensus.

That risk extends to AI safety itself. Researchers are already using AI agents to test frontier models for safety and alignment, expecting human review to serve as an independent check. But if experts unknowingly adopt an agent's bias on open-ended judgment calls, a misaligned system could end up steering the very research meant to expose its misalignment.

The team calls for ways to measure deference to AI agents in real work. Agents should make the best case for both sides, or ask experts for their own view before stating a position. Institutions need to decide which calls require independent human judgment and set aside time and resources for them.

"There may be no single right division of labor between people and AI. Some decisions may be fine to hand over, and others worth keeping. With the right tools, that split can be something we choose, instead of something we drift into," the researchers write.

## Previous studies point in the same direction

The findings add to recent research on how AI affects human judgment. A study on false confidence with 3,132 participants found that simply seeing AI answers nearly erased people's willingness to withhold judgment. In one part of the study, the share of people willing to say "I don't know" fell from 44 to 3 percent.

Presentation matters, too. When AI produced polished outputs such as code or documents, users checked facts less often, by 3.7 percentage points, questioned its reasoning less often, by 3.1 points, and missed missing context more often, by 5.2 points. Users who revised outputs step by step questioned the AI's reasoning 5.6 times more often than those who didn't iterate.

A Polish observational study of colonoscopies published in The Lancet Gastroenterology & Hepatology suggests that routine AI use at work can have lasting effects. After experienced doctors regularly used an AI system, their rate of finding precancerous lesions in exams without AI fell from 28.4 to 22.4 percent. That suggests people don't just adopt AI's perspective but may also lose some of their own cognitive skills.

A survey by Swiss Business School found a strong negative link between AI tool use and critical thinking, mainly among people ages 17 to 25. A solid education appeared to offer some protection, as people with higher degrees questioned AI answers more and engaged more with complex thought processes.

These findings come from early studies and snapshots, and other results point in a different direction. A pilot project in Nigeria found that students who used a chatbot as a virtual tutor twice a week made learning gains in just six weeks equal to nearly two extra years of learning.

title: Deepgram acquires Pipecat-maker Daily to bolster its voice AI infrastructure
excerpt: With Pipecat, Deepgram will likely gain a deeper understanding of real-time voice and video infrastructure.
title_en: Deepgram acquires Pipecat-maker Daily to bolster its voice AI infrastructure
excerpt_en: With Pipecat, Deepgram will likely gain a deeper understanding of real-time voice and video infrastructure.
content_en:
The voice AI sector is hot, and top players are trying to consolidate their position as more business models come to the fore through partnerships and acquisitions. Deepgram is the latest to make such moves: The company said on Thursday that it is acquiring Daily, the maker and maintainer of one of the most popular open source voice AI infrastructures, Pipecat.

The companies didn’t disclose the deal amount but said that they will keep Pipecat open source.

For the uninitiated, Pipecat is a framework that manages voice and video streams along with other pieces in the pipeline, like speech-to-text (STT), large language models (LLMs), and text-to-speech (TTS) models while reducing latency. Its maker, Daily, provides hosted infrastructure for voice and video calls of any kind.

With Pipecat, Deepgram will likely gain a deeper understanding of real-time voice and video infrastructure.

Daily has raised over $62 million in funding to date from investors such as Tiger Global, Highfield Capital, Nat Friedman, Lachy Groom, and Kevin Weil, according to PitchBook data. Earlier this year, Deepgram reached unicorn status with a $130 million Series C round. Incidentally, both companies were in the same Y Combinator batch in 2016.

Kwindla Kramer, Daily’s co-founder, said around the time when GPT-4 came out, the company started experimenting with AI-to-human communication over voice and text, which eventually resulted in the Pipecat framework. He noted that while there has been a lot of acquisition interest, he favored Deepgram’s CEO Scott Stephenson’s commitment to keeping Pipecat open source forever, and the engineering culture of both organizations matched, giving Daily’s team the freedom to work on different parts of the stack within a bigger organization.

“Scott was super committed to Pipecat being open source and vendor-neutral forever. I think there is both a personal commitment and commercial driver there. If you sit in the middle of an ecosystem that’s growing very fast, and have many parts of that ecosystem that are genuinely the best from your company, then everything being as open as possible is like a commercial advantage,” Kramer told TechCrunch.

Stephenson said that Deepgram has been wanting to work in open source for a long time, and the company realized that an orchestration framework for agents was a potential area, which drove the decision to partner with Daily.

“We want to open up the ecosystem so everybody can build voice agents. It’s great if you’re using Deepgram models, but I want you to be using the best models for your use case. And if Deepgram notices that we have some ground to catch up on in a certain area for our own models and products, that’s great. We want you to use partners, and then we’ll also work on becoming better in those areas,” he said.

Stephenson said the acquisition lets developers build agents with expressivity and end-to-end speech systems by plugging in different models and a context bus that connects all parts.

For Deepgram, the deal also lets it explore areas beyond voice through Pipecat, as the framework caters to real-time communication in different formats.

“We never thought about Pipecat as a voice toolkit. We thought about it as the toolkit we needed to build this new kind of AI-native software. Because of where we came from, we just always assumed real-time,” Kramer said.

Deepgram is also launching Real-Time Context Standard (RCS), an open protocol for voice agents that it co-developed with the Pipecat team. The protocol defines metadata like context from the audio, like a whisper, instructions for a language model on how it can use those signals, and guidance on how the response should sound.

Voice AI has seen a lot of investment from both the model and the infrastructure sides. Model makers like ElevenLabs, Gradium, and Fish Audio have raised millions of dollars. On the other hand, infrastructure companies like LiveKit and Vapi have raised multimillion-dollar funding rounds this year.

title: AWS will be a $1T business, Jassy says. But first, it will spend big.
excerpt: Amazon wants to be the king of AI cloud computing and become the first $1 trillion revenue business. But to do that it will have to continue on its capex spending spree, its CEO said Thursday.
title_en: AWS will be a $1T business, Jassy says. But first, it will spend big.
excerpt_en: Amazon wants to be the king of AI cloud computing and become the first $1 trillion revenue business. But to do that it will have to continue on its capex spending spree, its CEO said Thursday.
content_en:
Andy Jassy has made it known that he believes AWS can be a trillion-dollar revenue business. During Amazon’s quarterly earnings call on Thursday, he repeated this ambition.

“What we’re building at Amazon is unlike anything that’s ever been seen before. There has never been a business with a trillion dollars of annual revenue,” he said.

However, before the cloud business gets there, Amazon is going to have ramp up its capital expenditures to build out the infrastructure necessary to support that blossoming business.

“We still expect 2026 cash capex of approximately $220 billion — the majority for AWS — and expect to spend meaningfully more in 2027, with a clear line of sight to attract its financial returns,” Jassy revealed on Thursday.

Amazon’s big spending on its AI infrastructure buildout has been an ongoing source of concern for investors this year. Indeed, during Thursday’s call, Wall Street analysts repeatedly asked Jassy to explain the spending, the signals that the growth really will come, and the profit margins expected.

Jassy told them it was all money well spent because the e-commerce giant planned to capitalize on a historic moment in global cloud demand driven by AI. AWS revenue increased 39 percent from the year-ago quarter, a trend of steady growth for the sixth straight quarter.

And the CEO forecast on the call that it would increase by 40% not just next year, but in 2028, too.

“AWS is a $184 billion annualized revenue run-rate business, and yet the opportunity remains extraordinary,” the CEO enthused. “With our continued pace of innovation, new core and AI functionality, enterprises wanting to run their core and AI workloads in AWS, and the amount of capacity that we’re adding each year, we believe that AWS can grow north of 40 percent in each 2027 and in 2028, and be a trillion-dollar revenue business in the next five to 10 years.”

Jassy added that the company was “in the very early days” of AI adoption by the enterprise and said that, so far, the “strategy is working.”

Later, when questioned why the investment needed to grow AWS was so substantial, Jassy characterized the AI boom as a “once in a lifetime opportunity” that required, and was worth, such a big financial commitment now.

“We’re going to invest to continue being the leader,” he said. “We can fund this plan, and I think it will forever change the size of Amazon. It will forever change our revenue.”

Investors, however, remained concerned. Shares were down about 6% on Thursday in after-market trading.

The AI boom has been a mixed blessing for the cloud industry, since the AI services that undergird the boom are supported by cloud infrastructure. Like Amazon, other cloud providers are spending big but also earning big. Microsoft, for instance, just posted yet more record-breaking revenue growth, driven largely by its cloud business. It, too, has spent a bundle.

### Wabi reels in $55M for its consumer-focused AI assistant

Wabi Inc., the developer of an artificial intelligence assistant for consumers, today announced that it has raised $55 million in funding.

IVP led the seed round with contributions from Amazon Alexa Fund, Andreessen Horowitz and Forerunner. They were joined by a group of angel investors that included Salesforce Inc. CEO Marc Benioff and Shopify Inc. CEO Tobi Lütke. Wabi is now valued at $1.25 billion.

San Francisco-based Wabi was launched last year by serial AI entrepreneur Eugenia Kuyda. She previously founded Replika Inc., another consumer AI startup that had more than 35 million users as of last November. Wabi disclosed today that it’s seeing “strong early demand” but didn’t share specific user base numbers.

The company’s service is accessible via Mac, iOS and Android clients. Its interface is built around a group chat tool with an embedded AI assistant. If a group of friends uses a chat session to organize a meet-up, the AI assistant can find nearby restaurants that could serve as a suitable venue. It customizes its suggestions based on conversation details such as the time at which the participants agreed to meet.

The assistant can also make use of information stored in other apps. An integration with Plaid, a financial data sharing platform, enables Wabi to generate personal budgets and flag unused subscriptions that the user should cancel. A Gmail connector powers an alerting feature that notifies consumers about important messages.

Wabi’s AI assistant doubles as a vibe coding tool. Users can create simple apps to automate tasks such as managing to-do lists and planning events. The AI is also capable of generating simple, two-dimensional games that run directly in the chat window.

The chat interface is flanked by a sidebar that contains widgets relevant to the conversation. If a user is planning a trip, Wabi might display flight departure and arrival dates. Restaurant recommendations appear in vertically organized cards that each contain a photo of a venue’s exterior and a brief description.

“We believe Wabi has the power to become an operating system for life, a place where your people, your tools, and your AI come together to help you do more of what matters,” Kuyda said.

If Wabi proves popular among consumers, large market players could decide to launch similar services. Such competition may require the startup to find additional ways of differentiating its software. Some vibe coding startups have trained custom AI models to set their tools apart from more popular alternatives such as OpenAI Group PBC’s Codex.

Wabi will invest the proceeds from its funding round in growth and product development initiatives. The company’s near-term priorities include the launch of a Windows app.

### HPE cuts executive status meetings with no-code apps built on monday.com

Enterprises are learning that no-code apps deliver the most value when the people closest to the work build them. As AI agents arrive inside work management platforms, the harder task is getting employees comfortable enough to use them without letting adoption spin out of control.

That shift is playing out at Hewlett Packard Enterprise Co., which runs workflows across the company on monday.com Ltd.’s AI work platform. One early tester turned a single IT ticketing build, assembled in 24 hours, into a companywide practice of teaching colleagues to build their own workflows, according to Kate Kenner (pictured), capability and community lead for strategic sourcing and planning at HPE.

“My thing is, I love building things, I do, but I want to enable them to build it,” Kenner said. “So a lot of times, I’ll sit with them and be like, well, I think you have the skills to build this because it’s such an easy product. It really doesn’t take a lot of uplift to learn it.”

Kenner spoke with Rebecca Knight at monday.com’s Elevate event, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how HPE scales no-code apps, how it governs AI use and how agents are taking on routine reporting. *(\* Disclosure below.)*

### Scaling no-code apps and AI with guardrails

Enthusiasm for AI isn’t the problem. Research from monday.com and Nielsen, cited by Knight, found that 72% of people work at companies that mandate or strongly encourage AI use, even as the processes around it lag. At HPE, admins pace the rollout by training users first and giving groups separate AI credit allotments, Kenner explained.

“It’s really tough. But you got to give enough allowance for people to be creative and to get their hands wet … But also not let them go wild, wild west on it,” she said.

HPE is also building vibe apps with monday vibe, monday.com’s no-code tool for creating custom applications. Kenner’s first one replaced the chore of pasting charts into slides with an executive dashboard that can still export to PowerPoint for leaders who want a deck.

“It’s a no-code solution that we pair with so many of our boards to build the dashboards we want,” she said. “In our corporate world, I will say everyone loves PowerPoint and it has been very hard to get off PowerPoint.”

The payoff showed up on the calendar. With live project status available anytime, executives cut back their review meetings, while a finalize button archives each month’s numbers as a system of record, according to Kenner.

“They knocked a whole bunch of the meetings off the calendar,” Kenner said. “Instead of weekly, now they’re monthly.”

Those no-code apps now pair with AI agents that take on the grunt work. Each week, an agent Kenner configured pulls attendance for her Monday livestream from Microsoft Corp.’s Teams, maps attendees by organization, region and manager, and flags anyone missing from HR records.

“I basically programmed it and every Monday I just hit run and she’ll go through all of it and she’ll come back with any of the things that may be flagged,” Kenner said.

title: As search traffic dries up, Reddit announces it’s shifting to a logged-in experience
excerpt: As AI transforms how people find information online, Reddit is rethinking its open-web roots to protect its audience and business.
title_en: As search traffic dries up, Reddit announces it’s shifting to a logged-in experience
excerpt_en: As AI transforms how people find information online, Reddit is rethinking its open-web roots to protect its audience and business.
content_en:
Reddit has long attracted millions of users to its site through Google, with many even appending the word “Reddit” to their search queries for better answers. But as search traffic dries up amid the shift to AI-powered search, Reddit is rethinking its relationship with the open internet. In its third-quarter earnings call on Thursday, the company announced it’s transitioning to a primarily “logged-in experience.”

The move is designed to protect its data from AI scraping, allowing the company to instead forge lucrative licensing deals with model providers. But just as important, such a shift could help Reddit to increase its revenue even as it faces daily active user declines in its largest market, the U.S.

Overall, Reddit’s global daily active users were flat quarter-over-quarter in Q3, reaching 130.3 million, while U.S. daily active users dropped from 53.2 million in Q2 to 50.7 million in Q3 and were down 2% year-over-year.

The company is not alone in seeing such declines; the shift to an AI-centered web has impacted most websites and publishers by now, leading to fewer click-throughs, as AI summaries provide answers that don’t require website visits and Google’s traditional “ten blue links” have reduced relevance. (The change is now even impacting Google’s bottom line, its earnings revealed.)

But at Reddit’s scale, the numbers associated with such a decline are enormous. The company said search traffic referrals dropped by more than 1 million referrals on average per week in October. It warned that if the trend continues, daily active users could decline to a low-double-digit percentage by next quarter. (To play that out: a hypothetical 10% to 12% decline could bring Reddit to roughly 115 million to 117 million daily actives, down from 130.3 million in Q3. That’s a huge drop!)

At the same time, Reddit has gotten significantly better at monetizing its audience even as its growth weakens. Revenue increased 53% year-over-year to $895 million, ahead of Wall Street’s expectations of about $875 million. Net income rose 74% to $283 million. Advertising revenue grew 54% to $847 million while nonadvertising revenue, which includes its AI data-licensing business, grew 35% year-over-year to $48 million.

And despite a 2% year-over-year decline in U.S. daily users, Reddit’s average revenue per daily active user in the U.S. rose 53% to $13.82. Globally, average revenue per daily active user increased 36% year-over-year to $6.87.

Shifting to a logged-in experience could boost those numbers even higher because logged-in users are typically worth more to advertisers.

Unlike the logged-out users who often find their way to the site via search, logged-in users provide more signals about their interests and behaviors, which helps to better target and personalize ads.

Those same signals would also help Reddit provide a more personalized experience to its users, which includes personalized feeds, recommendations of new communities to subscribe to, and pushes to vote, comment, participate, and more. (This also includes pushing recommendations to its new algorithmic “For You” feed, announced yesterday, which will combine posts from communities users belong to alongside other recommendations based on their interests.)

Still, a change of this magnitude could be the canary in the coal mine for the open web.

“I don’t know about you, but as someone whose life has been defined by the open internet, it’s a big change for me,” wrote Reddit co-founder and CEO Steve Huffman in a post published on Reddit’s site. “But I’ve come to the conclusion that this is the right decision for our platform and the right decision for our business,” he said.

The company notes that the shift to the logged-in experience will not be an overnight change; it will first run tests in select markets outside the U.S. in the fourth quarter. It doesn’t yet have a timeline for when the change will be rolled out to all its users worldwide. It also acknowledged that access to a logged-out front page is important.

Plus, Reddit pointed out that being logged in doesn’t mean having to give up anonymity, nor will it remove its option to browse anonymously through its “incognito mode” experience, which is being rebuilt.

“There are still plenty of questions that are unanswered, particularly around where the boundaries should be between logged-in and logged-out experiences,” Hoffman wrote. “This is a big evolution for Reddit, and not one we’re taking lightly. But I believe it’s the right next step for the platform and for our future.”

title_en: ServiceNow shares plunge 27% to worst day ever after earnings revive AI disruption fears
excerpt_en: ServiceNow's stock recorded its worst day ever on underwhelming third-quarter results.
content_en:
ServiceNow shares sank 27% on Thursday and recorded their worst day on record after the enterprise software company's third-quarter results underwhelmed, reigniting artificial intelligence disruption concerns.

"This was a little bit uncharacteristic for ServiceNow standards, just in terms of the lack of upside," Citi's Tyler Radke told CNBC on Thursday.

Revenue grew more than 20% during the period to $4.11 billion, which was roughly in line with a $4.10 billion estimate from analysts polled by LSEG. Adjusted earnings came up short at $1.00 per share, compared to a forecast of $1.02.

The results did little to overturn recent "SaaSpocalypse" fears, or concerns that new AI capabilities will upend traditional software business models.

The stock drop came even after the company slightly lifted its full-year 2026 subscription revenue outlook to between $15.78 billion and $15.79 billion. Net new AI average contract value jumped 65%.

One factor spooking investors is the lack of immediate payoff for the company's investments in its newly formed forward-deployed engineering team that embeds in enterprises to build AI solutions, Radke said.

"It's just going to be a little bit longer of a waiting game, and so I think the market, you know, wanted to see something a little bit sooner," he said. "I think you got to wait until next year to really see that inflection."

### Brakes built for speed: Why least privilege lets monday.com’s AI teams move faster

As AI agents spread across enterprise workflows, permission management is becoming one of the most practical levers for keeping them safe. Agents act with the access people give them, so the old problem of sprawling privileges now plays out at machine speed.

Governance is often cast as a brake on that momentum, especially as work platforms build agents into everyday tools. The view at monday.com Ltd., which relaunched as an AI work platform with native agents, is that well-designed guardrails let teams move faster, according to Ryan Nigro (pictured), security trust and enablement team lead at monday.com.

“The brakes on a car are not for you to be slowing down constantly,” Nigro said. “It’s so that you could feel confident in going faster.”

Nigro spoke with theCUBE’s Rebecca Knight at monday.com’s Elevate event, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how permission management is key to AI agent safety. *(\* Disclosure below.)*

### Permission management as the core of AI governance

Nigro’s approach rests on least privilege, a concept cybersecurity teams first applied to human users. AI largely does what employees already do, so haywire permissions for people become a problem for agents too, he explained. The fix is to roll out AI piece by piece, granting each tool the minimum access it needs and expanding as results prove out.

“You don’t want to enable all the features and give everybody all the access all at once. That’s just bad permissions,” Nigro said.

Everyday personnel moves create some of the biggest gaps. An employee who shifts from finance to legal can end up holding both departments’ access at companies without strict permission management, Nigro noted. He cited an IBM Corp. study estimating that 80% to 90% of breaches stem from human error tied to over-permissioning.

“It just comes to making sure that your users are properly being given just enough to do their roles but not too much to cause harm,” Nigro said. “There’s no reason why a sales rep should have the ability to change your production environment.”

### Monday.com bets on deployment experts to turn AI agents into real returns

Enterprises have embraced AI for everyday tasks, but turning autonomous agents into measurable business returns is proving far harder. The bottleneck is no longer the technology but the organizational change needed to rewire processes around it.

Software providers are responding by pairing their platforms with hands-on guidance. Since monday.com Ltd. relaunched as an AI work platform, its customers have asked less about what the technology can do and more about how to make it pay off, according to Eran Zinman (pictured), co-founder and co-chief executive officer of monday.com.

“I think what’s hard is the actual business change you have to go through,” Zinman said. “Eventually companies want to see return on investment. Tokens cost a lot of money. You want to see a real impact on your business.”

Zinman spoke with theCUBE’s Rebecca Knight at monday.com’s Elevate event, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed the challenge of turning autonomous agents into measurable business returns. *(\* Disclosure below.)*

### Putting autonomous agents to work starts at home

Before asking customers to change, the company tested the change on itself. Under an initiative called Customer Zero, employees set aside their regular jobs for a week and competed to build agents, Zinman explained.

“We said we’re going to stop the company for one week. We literally have done that. Nobody was doing their regular job for a week,” Zinman said. “Everybody was building agents.”

The exercise produced more than 3,600 agents, and about 2,000 are still running, according to Zinman. That playbook now underpins monday Frontier, a new organization that combines managed services and deployment engineers to help customers find bottlenecks and launch AI projects within weeks.

“Adopting AI really requires expertise. I know how hard it is because we experienced ourselves that you have this amazing technology, but how do you actually use it?” Zinman said.

The company is also rebranding as simply monday, reflecting a product built around people and agents sharing one workspace. Zinman rejects predictions that AI will push humans out of the workforce, insisting accountability stays with people.

“AI will never take responsibility for what you’re doing in your business,” Zinman said. “And you need people in the loop. I feel the best combination to adopt AI is people and agents working together where AI is not replacing people; it’s empowering people.”
